fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the heart of Charles H. Spurgeon’s message — that salvation is all of grace, from first to last, and is received by a single look of faith at Jesus Christ crucified. Twenty-one short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as a companion to Spurgeon’s own public-domain works, which readers are warmly encouraged to go to directly.
fields.about_html:
This is not a book by Charles H. Spurgeon. It is a companion to him — an independent work of exposition and appreciation, written by Ochorus, that gathers the heart of the Prince of Preachers’ teaching into twenty-one short chapters for the ordinary reader, with a chapter on his life before them and a guide to his books after.

Spurgeon’s one message was the one that saved him as a boy of fifteen in a Colchester chapel: Look unto me, and be ye saved. Everything he preached for forty years — free grace and the free offer of the gospel, the substitution of Christ, simple faith and the repentance that goes with it, the unchanging God, the promises, prayer, the war with sin, the happiness of religion, songs in the night, communion at the Lord’s Table, the winning of souls, the care of the orphan, and the contending for truth that darkened his last years — is that one look applied. This volume follows the thread, is honest about his combativeness and the limits of his system, and ends each chapter where he would have ended it: in a few searching questions and a prayer.

Spurgeon’s own writings are in the public domain and freely available, and many are in the Ochorus library; every chapter here names them so the reader can go to the source. This companion is offered only to open the door. It quotes Scripture from the Authorised (King James) Version, the Bible Spurgeon preached from, and makes no claim to stand in for his own vivid, Christ-filled pages.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else. ISAIAH 45:22

Of all the preachers in this series, Charles Haddon Spurgeon needs the least introduction and is the most often misremembered. He is quoted everywhere, often in sentences he never quite said. He preached to congregations of five and six thousand in London every Sunday for more than thirty years, without amplification, and his sermons were printed each week and sold by the tens of thousands across the English-speaking world and far beyond it. He founded a college for preachers, an orphanage, almshouses and a society for carrying Christian books to the poor. He wrote a seven-volume commentary on the Psalms and a pair of daily devotionals that have never been out of print. And he did it all before he died, worn out, at fifty-seven.

The scale of the man can hide the substance, which is remarkably simple.

One look

Spurgeon’s teaching begins where his Christian life began: in a small chapel in Colchester on a snowy January morning in 1850, when a fifteen-year-old boy heard a lay preacher repeat a single text from Isaiah and urge him to look to Christ. He looked, and he was saved, and for the next forty years he did very little else but tell other people to do the same. In All of Grace, the small book he wrote for enquirers late in his life, he put it in a single sentence: when he heard the command to look, he says, “I looked, and in a moment the Lord justified me.”

That is the one thread that runs through everything in this book. Salvation is all of grace, from its first cause in the eternal love of God to its last stone laid in heaven, and grace is received by the simplest act a sinner can perform: a look of trust at Jesus Christ crucified. Spurgeon was a convinced Calvinist who believed that God chooses, calls and keeps His people. He was also one of the most urgent evangelists of his century, who pleaded with every hearer, without exception, to come to Christ that very morning. He saw no contradiction between the two, and he refused to let either swallow the other. Both served the same end. The sovereignty of grace meant that salvation depended on nothing in the sinner, so that anybody might look; the free offer meant that nobody need wait to find something in himself before he looked.

For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God. EPHESIANS 2:8

Everything else he taught flows from that fountain. The cross is the object at which faith looks. Prayer is the looking turned into asking. The promises are God’s pledges to people who look to Him. Affliction drives the eye back to Christ when it has wandered. The Lord’s Supper sets Christ before the eye every week. Soul-winning is the work of telling others where to look. Even his last great controversy was, in his own mind, a quarrel about whether the churches would go on pointing people to the same place.

How this book is arranged

After a chapter on his life, twenty-one short chapters set out his teaching. They begin with his conversion and the gospel it gave him: the look of faith, justification of the ungodly, the substitution of Christ, and his conviction that every sermon must lead to the cross. They go on to the two great truths he held together, free grace and the free offer, and then to faith and repentance, the unchanging God on whom faith rests, the promises, prayer, the Word and the Spirit. They move from there into the life of the believer: the warfare with sin, the perseverance of the saints, the gladness of the Christian life and the dark night of affliction, and communion with Christ at His table. The last follow him out to the lost and the poor, into the controversy of his final years, and home to heaven.

Each chapter ends with application points and a prayer. Spurgeon would have wanted it so. He preached for verdicts, and almost every sermon he ever delivered turns, near the end, to face the hearer with a direct question. Read one chapter a day, or one a week. Linger over the application points. Pray the prayer, or better, pray your own.

Reading him with care

This is not a book of hero-worship, and there are places where Spurgeon must be read carefully. Four deserve to be named at the outset.

First, his Calvinism. Spurgeon believed the doctrines of grace were simply the gospel, and he could say so in terms that will jar readers who belong to other traditions. Many sincere Christians who love Christ read the passages on election differently, and they are not enemies of grace. This book presents his convictions as he held them, but it tries to show that the heart of what he taught — that salvation is God’s gift and not our achievement — is common ground for every believer who has ever sung of amazing grace.

Second, his combativeness. Spurgeon was a controversialist by temperament as well as conviction. His sermon on baptismal regeneration in 1864 and the Down-Grade controversy of 1887 were both fought with a sharpness that wounded friends as well as opponents. Chapter twenty-two weighs that honestly.

Third, his temperament. He was a man of high spirits and deep glooms, of sparkling humour and sudden depression. His rhetoric belongs to the Victorian pulpit, with its long periods, its thunder and its tears, and it does not always travel well.

Fourth, sheer bulk. More than three and a half thousand of his sermons are in print. Nobody can read them all. The chapters that follow try to draw out the handful of truths he returned to again and again, and the Reader’s Guide at the end suggests where to begin.

So the counsel of this book is the counsel of Scripture: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Where Spurgeon is faithful — and on the cross, on faith, on prayer, on the preciousness of Christ, he is faithful indeed — receive it and act on it. Where he presses further than Scripture warrants, or speaks more harshly than love requires, mark it and pass on. He would have been the first to insist on it. He wanted nobody to look at him.

In the little book he addressed to seekers, he likened his work to a drinking fountain set up by the roadside, and he answered his critics with one sentence that might stand over the whole of his ministry: “Here is my fountain, and here is my cup: find fault if you please; but do drink of the water of life.” That is the spirit in which this companion is offered. It is not a substitute for his own pages, which are freely available and still vivid. It is a cup hung beside the fountain.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Before reading further, write down in one sentence what you would say to someone who asked you how to be saved. Keep it, and compare it with Spurgeon’s answer when you reach the end of this book.

2. Notice whether you come to Spurgeon expecting a doctrine to defend or a Saviour to look at. Ask God for the second.

3. If you belong to a tradition that differs from his on election, resolve to listen for what you share with him before you listen for what divides you.

4. Choose one of his books from the Ochorus library — All of Grace is the best place to start — and read a chapter alongside each chapter of this one.

5. Ask yourself honestly when you last looked to Christ for yourself, rather than simply thinking about Him.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You said, Look unto Me, and be saved, and I have spent a great deal of time looking elsewhere.
I have looked at my feelings, at my progress, at my failures and at other people’s opinions of me. Turn my eyes back to You.
As I read of a man whose whole life pointed away from himself to You, keep me from admiring the pointer and missing the One he pointed to.
Teach me that all is of grace, and let me drink from the fountain, not merely study the cup. Amen.

fields.title: The Boy Under the Gallery
fields.body_html:
For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:2

A manse full of Puritans. Charles Haddon Spurgeon was born on the nineteenth of June, 1834, at Kelvedon in Essex, the eldest child of John Spurgeon, a clerk who also preached to a small Independent congregation, and his wife Eliza. For much of his early childhood the boy lived with his grandparents at Stambourne, where his grandfather James Spurgeon was the Independent minister for more than fifty years. The old manse had a room full of Puritan books, and the child who would one day be called the last of the Puritans learned to read among them. He first read Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress there, and he never left the company of those old writers. He grew up knowing the doctrines of grace, the catechism and the Bible. What he did not have was peace.

A snowstorm in Colchester. By his mid-teens the conviction of sin had grown into misery. He went from chapel to chapel looking for someone who would tell him how a sinner could be right with God, and heard, as he later remembered it, a great deal about duty and very little about Christ. On Sunday the sixth of January, 1850, a snowstorm turned him aside from the chapel he meant to attend and into a small Primitive Methodist chapel in Artillery Street, Colchester. The minister had not arrived. A thin layman, a working man with little education, went up into the pulpit and preached on the only text he seems to have had: Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth (Isaiah 45:22). After some minutes he ran out of material, fixed his eye on the pale young stranger sitting under the gallery, and told him he looked miserable and would always be miserable unless he obeyed the text. Then he shouted at him to look to Jesus Christ. Spurgeon looked. The burden he had carried for years went, and he said all his life that he had seen the sun that morning. Everything he ever taught begins in that chapel.

Baptist, preacher, pastor. Although raised among paedobaptist Independents, he became convinced from the New Testament that baptism belongs to believers, and he was baptised by immersion in the River Lark at Isleham on the third of May, 1850. He moved to Cambridge as a schoolmaster’s assistant, joined a Baptist church there, and began to teach in its Sunday school. That autumn he was sent to a cottage meeting at Teversham, assuming someone else was to preach, and discovered on the road that the preacher was to be himself. He was sixteen. Within a year he was pastor of the little Baptist chapel at Waterbeach, a rough village outside Cambridge, and the chapel filled. He never went to university or college. An opportunity to meet the tutor of a Baptist college came to nothing through a misunderstanding over a room, and as he walked away he believed he heard a word of Scripture pressed on his mind: Seekest thou great things for thyself? seek them not (Jeremiah 45:5). He took it as settling the matter, and he never regretted it.

London. In the winter of 1853 he was invited to preach at New Park Street Chapel in Southwark, a historic Baptist congregation that had dwindled to a remnant in a building meant for many more. He was nineteen. By the spring of 1854 he was its pastor, and within months the chapel could not hold the crowds. It was enlarged, and still could not. The congregation hired Exeter Hall on the Strand, and then the great Music Hall in the Surrey Gardens. From 1855 his sermons were printed every week, and they were soon being read in America, Australia and across the British Empire. The newspapers mocked him as a vulgar boy, a clown and a sensation. He kept the cuttings, and went on preaching Christ crucified in plain words to people who had never heard it put so they could understand it.

Susannah. In January 1856 he married Susannah Thompson, a member of the New Park Street congregation who had first thought the young preacher rather unpolished. The marriage was deeply happy. Their twin sons, Thomas and Charles, were born in September that year, and both became ministers. For most of their married life Susannah was an invalid, and much of it she spent at home in pain; yet from her room she ran a Book Fund that sent thousands of volumes of theology to poor ministers who could not afford them.

The night at the Surrey Gardens. On the nineteenth of October, 1856, a month after the twins were born, Spurgeon preached for the first time in the Surrey Gardens Music Hall to a crowd of perhaps twelve thousand, with thousands more outside. Early in the service someone raised a false cry of fire. In the panic on the stairs seven people were killed and many injured. Spurgeon was twenty-two. He was taken away almost prostrate, and for days he was sunk in a grief so deep that some feared for his mind. He recovered through a verse — Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him (Philippians 2:9) — which turned his thoughts from his own wreck to the honour of Christ. But the darkness of that night never entirely left him, and he suffered from recurring depression for the rest of his life.

The Tabernacle. In March 1861 the congregation moved into the Metropolitan Tabernacle at the Elephant and Castle, built to seat some five thousand and often holding more. He preached there twice every Sunday for thirty years. Around the pulpit grew a great web of work. The Pastors’ College, begun in 1856 with a single student, trained hundreds of men, many of them poor and ill-schooled as he had been. The Colportage Association carried Bibles and good books into villages. The Stockwell Orphanage, founded in 1867 after a widow named Anne Hillyard offered him a large gift for the purpose, received fatherless boys and later girls. There were almshouses for poor widows, mission halls, Sunday schools and a monthly magazine, The Sword and the Trowel. He wrote The Treasury of David, a commentary on the Psalms in seven volumes, over some twenty years, and the daily readings later gathered as Morning and Evening. His brother James came to share the pastoral load. The prayer meeting beneath the platform, he insisted, was the engine of it all.

Pain and controversy. From his mid-thirties he suffered from gout and a kidney disease that laid him aside for weeks at a time, and in later years he spent part of most winters at Menton on the French Riviera, trying to recover strength. He was also a fighter. In 1864 his sermon against baptismal regeneration provoked a storm with evangelical clergy in the Church of England and cost him his place in the Evangelical Alliance. In 1887, alarmed by what he saw as a slide in the churches away from the inspiration of Scripture, the atonement and eternal judgement, he published warnings in The Sword and the Trowel under the name the Down Grade, and in October that year withdrew from the Baptist Union. In January 1888 the Union’s council passed a vote of censure on him. Friends parted from him, among them some of his own former students, and he felt it bitterly. The Cheque Book of the Bank of Faith, which he began in those months, speaks of being cast into deep waters.

Home. His last sermon at the Tabernacle was preached in June 1891. He fell desperately ill that summer, rallied, and went to Menton in the autumn with Susannah. He died there on the thirty-first of January, 1892, at the age of fifty-seven. His body was brought back to London, tens of thousands filed past the coffin, and he was buried at West Norwood Cemetery. On the coffin lay his Bible, open at the verse from Isaiah that had once been preached to a miserable boy under the gallery in Colchester.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Spurgeon was saved through a sermon preached badly by an untrained man. Thank God this week for someone who pointed you to Christ without polish, and tell them if you can.

2. He took the verse from Jeremiah as a check on his ambition. Is there a great thing you are seeking for yourself? Bring it honestly before God.

3. The Surrey Gardens disaster left a wound that never fully healed. Name a sorrow you have tried to pretend is behind you, and bring it to Christ rather than hiding it.

4. Around his pulpit grew colleges, orphanages and almshouses. Ask what one practical work of mercy your own faith should be producing.

5. Notice how much of his life was carried by others — Susannah, his brother, the praying people beneath the platform. Pray today for someone whose work depends on your prayers.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You met a miserable boy in a snowstorm and told him to look, and he looked and lived.
I thank You that You need no polished preachers and no perfect circumstances to save a soul. You need only to be lifted up.
Keep me from seeking great things for myself. Give me instead a heart that is glad to point away from itself to You.
And when my own nights come, as his did, keep me looking where he looked, until I see You face to face. Amen.

fields.title: Look unto Me
fields.body_html:
And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life. JOHN 3:14–15

Spurgeon told the story of his conversion more often than any other, not because it was remarkable but because it was ordinary. A miserable teenager heard a poor sermon on a short text and did what the text said. In Spurgeon’s view nothing more is ever needed.

The years of looking elsewhere

He was not converted from irreligion. He was raised in a devout home, had read the old Puritans in his grandfather’s study, prayed, and was sincerely afraid of sin. For years none of it gave him any peace.

The reason, as he later understood it, is that he was looking in the wrong direction. He was looking at himself — at his repentance, to see if it was deep enough; at his feelings, to see if they were the right feelings; at his prayers, to see if they were earnest. In All of Grace he describes that time with painful honesty. He had heard the plan of salvation from childhood, he says, and yet understood it in his innermost soul no better than a heathen who had never heard it. The light was there. He was blind to it.

The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined. ISAIAH 9:2

Many earnest people live in exactly this condition. They are not careless but anxious, waiting for something to happen inside them before they dare to come to Christ — and it never quite happens, because they are watching the wrong place.

A look, and nothing more

What the lay preacher in Colchester did, without any skill, was to take the young man’s eyes off himself. The text was Isaiah 45:22, and its genius is in its verb. It does not say, Feel, or Do, or Become. It says, Look.

Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else. ISAIAH 45:22

Spurgeon loved to point out how little a look requires: no strength, no education, no money, no preparation. You do not have to be good to look. In the wilderness, when the people of Israel were dying of the serpents’ bites, God did not tell them to apply medicine or to reform their conduct. He told Moses to lift up a serpent of brass on a pole.

And it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived. NUMBERS 21:9

Our Lord Himself took up that story and applied it to His own death, and Spurgeon applied it to his own conversion. In All of Grace he writes that “Jesus Christ, made sin for me, was what I saw, and that sight gave me rest.” He goes on to say that the bitten Israelites were healed the instant they looked, and so was he when he looked to the crucified Saviour. In the Cheque Book he says it more simply still: “I looked to Jesus and lived at once. I know I did.”

Why a look saves

It would be possible to hear this as a cheap gospel, as if a glance could substitute for a changed life. Spurgeon did not mean that, and he was careful to say why a look saves.

It saves because of what it looks at. The saving power is not in the eye but in the object. A look at the brass serpent healed because God had appointed it; a look anywhere else did nothing. A look at Christ saves because He has done everything needed for the salvation of a sinner. The look adds nothing to His work. It simply receives it. That is why Spurgeon could insist that faith is not a work, and that the weakest faith in a strong Saviour saves as surely as the strongest.

Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world. JOHN 1:29

It saves, secondly, because it is a look away. The man who looks at Christ has, in that act, stopped looking at himself as the ground of his hope. Spurgeon thought this was the real difficulty for most people. The look is easy to perform and hard to consent to, because it requires us to abandon every other hope. In Around the Wicket Gate he says it is wicked to suppose that Christ has half saved us and left us to finish the work with some feeling or effort of our own.

And it saves, thirdly, because it is only the beginning of a lifetime of looking. Spurgeon never treated conversion as a ticket stamped and put away. The look that saves becomes the posture of the whole Christian life. In a passage gathered in Gleanings Among the Sheaves he urges the believer to look to Christ in every trial, every temptation and every failure, and adds: “He that looks at Christ walks safely.”

Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith. HEBREWS 12:2

Awakened is not saved

There is one caution Spurgeon pressed on anxious people, and it is still needed. Being troubled about your soul is a mercy, he says in Around the Wicket Gate, but it is not the same thing as being saved. He compares it to a man who wakes to find his house on fire and sits on the edge of the bed congratulating himself on being awake. The point of waking is to get out.

Some people make a home in their anxiety. They have been seeking for years, they are sincerely concerned, and they have come to treat their concern as if it were itself a kind of faith. Spurgeon was gentle with them and very direct. You do not need to be more troubled before you come. You do not need to feel your sin more deeply, or to understand the atonement better, or to be surer that you are one of the elect. You need to look now, at the One who is lifted up for you.

Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. JOHN 6:37

Nor did he pretend that looking always feels dramatic. His own experience happened to be vivid. He knew many whose faith came quietly, and he refused to make any particular feeling the test. The question is not how you felt when you looked, but where you are looking now.

The whole ends of the earth

One more thing in the text mattered to him. It is addressed to all the ends of the earth. The invitation is as wide as the world. Spurgeon was a Calvinist, and he believed that God had chosen His people before time began. But he never allowed that doctrine to narrow the invitation, because the text does not. He assumed that anyone listening was entitled to obey it. When his coffin was carried through London, the Bible on it lay open at this verse. He had spent his life lifting up the brass serpent and calling to dying people to look.

1. Where do you habitually look for assurance — to your feelings, your progress, your prayers? Name it honestly, then deliberately turn your attention to Christ crucified.

2. If you have been a seeker for a long time, ask whether you have made a home in your anxiety. Do not wait for more conviction. Look to Christ today.

3. Read Numbers 21:4–9 and John 3:14–16 together, and write down what the Israelites had to do, and what they did not have to do.

4. Each morning this week, before anything else, spend one minute looking at a passage about the cross, rather than at your plans for the day.

5. Tell someone else, in your own words, where to look. Spurgeon was saved by a man who had very little to say. You have enough.

Lord Jesus, lifted up for me as the serpent was lifted up in the wilderness, I look to You.
I have searched my own heart for some reason to hope, and found only more reasons to despair. I stop searching there.
You have done everything. Let me add nothing, and trust You for everything.
And let this look become the habit of my whole life, until I see You with no veil between. Amen.

fields.body_html:
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. ROMANS 4:5

When Spurgeon sat down to write a small book for people who were not yet Christians, he did not begin with the love of God, or the beauty of Christ, or the misery of sin. He began with a phrase from Romans that most readers pass over, and he called his first real chapter by its name: God Justifieth the Ungodly. He thought it the most astonishing sentence in the Bible, and he wanted every seeker to meet it before anything else.

An unlikely title

Notice what the verse does not say. It does not say that God justifies the godly, or the nearly godly, or the ungodly once they have improved. It says He justifies the ungodly, and it gives this to God as a kind of title. In All of Grace Spurgeon points out that the enemies of the gospel had long made this very charge against it — that it receives wicked people — and that Scripture, far from denying the charge, adopts it. God takes the name to Himself. The Lord, he writes, “comes, not because we are just, but to make us so: he justifieth the ungodly.”

This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief. 1 TIMOTHY 1:15

Most people, Spurgeon observed, carry in them a natural legality. We assume that God’s favour must follow some goodness in us, and so we either try to produce it or despair of producing it. Both responses keep the sinner away from Christ. The self-righteous man thinks he does not need justifying; the despairing man thinks he cannot be justified. The verse cuts across both. It is precisely the ungodly for whom the gospel is intended, and therefore nobody is too ungodly for it.

What the word means

Spurgeon was careful about the word justify, because a great deal depends on it. In a sermon on Romans 3:24, Justification by Grace, he explains that it is a courtroom word. To justify a man is not to make him better but to declare him righteous in the eye of the law. An earthly court can do this only if the accused is innocent. It can pardon a guilty man, but it cannot justify him. “The Queen may pardon him,” he says, “but she cannot justify him.” The crime remains his crime.

That is what makes the gospel so staggering. The verdict against us has been given, and it is guilty. And yet God justifies. In the same sermon he calls it the wonder of wonders “that we are proved guilty, and yet we are justified.” No earthly judge could do it without corrupting justice.

Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. ROMANS 3:24

The answer lies in the last words of that verse: through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. God does not declare the guilty righteous by pretending they are something they are not. He declares them righteous because the penalty of their sin has been borne by another, and the righteousness of that other is reckoned to them. The next chapter of this book is about that substitution. Here the point is simpler. Justification is a verdict, and it is God’s verdict. It rests on what Christ has done, not on what we have become.

It is God that justifieth

Spurgeon drew great comfort from Paul’s question at the end of Romans 8.

Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth. ROMANS 8:33

If you justify yourself, he says bluntly in All of Grace, you are simply deceiving yourself. If you ask other people to justify you, their verdict is worth very little; they will praise you for small favours and slander you for less. But if God justifies you, the matter is closed. There is no higher court. The accuser may bring his charges, and conscience may bring its memories, but the Judge Himself has pronounced.

He admitted that the truth astonished him personally. “None but God would ever have thought of justifying me,” he writes. “I am a wonder to myself.” He pointed to Saul of Tarsus, the persecutor, who became the greatest preacher of justification by faith. Nobody but God would have thought of justifying such a man. Nobody but God could have done it.

Why this is good news for you

The practical force of the doctrine, as Spurgeon pressed it, is that it makes the gospel available now, to anyone. If God justifies the ungodly, then you qualify. You do not have to wait until you are better, because the gospel is not addressed to the better. You do not have to wait until you feel forgiven, because justification is a verdict given in heaven, not a sensation produced in you.

Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. ISAIAH 1:18

Spurgeon knew that some would hear this as licence: if God justifies the ungodly, why not stay ungodly? He answered the objection a few chapters later in All of Grace, in Concerning Deliverance from Sinning, and his answer is worth holding alongside this one. The God who justifies also renews. The same grace that gives the verdict gives a new heart, and a person who has truly been forgiven so much does not want to go back to what nearly destroyed him. Justification is not the whole of salvation. But it is the door, and the door is open to the ungodly.

A word of honest qualification

Christians have understood justification in different ways, and Spurgeon stood firmly in the Reformation tradition that sees it as a legal declaration grounded in Christ’s righteousness reckoned to the believer. Some readers will frame it differently. What almost every Christian tradition confesses, however, is the heart of Spurgeon’s point: that we do not earn God’s acceptance, and that grace comes to the undeserving. He could also sound, in places, as if assurance should follow immediately and completely on believing, and some sensitive souls have been troubled because theirs did not. He knew better elsewhere, and he was tender with the doubting. The verdict does not depend on the feeling of it.

There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus. ROMANS 8:1
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read Romans 4:1–8 slowly. Underline every phrase that tells you what God does and every phrase that tells you what man does not do.

2. Ask yourself which of the two errors you lean towards: thinking you do not need justifying, or thinking you cannot be justified. Confess it by name.

3. When your conscience accuses you this week, answer it with Romans 8:33–34 rather than with a list of your recent good behaviour.

4. Think of someone you have privately written off as too far gone. Pray for them by name, remembering Saul of Tarsus.

5. Write down, in one sentence, the difference between being pardoned and being justified, and thank God for both.

A PRAYER
Holy Father, I am ungodly, and I have spent too long pretending otherwise or despairing because of it.
I bring You no goodness of my own. I believe on You who justifieth the ungodly, and I rest in the verdict You have given for Christ’s sake.
When the accuser speaks, let me answer with Your word: It is God that justifieth.
And let the wonder of it make me humble, grateful and glad to live for You. Amen.

fields.title: The Sin-Bearer
fields.body_html:
Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed. 1 PETER 2:24

If the last chapter asked how God can justify the ungodly, this one gives Spurgeon’s answer. It is the answer he gave in almost every sermon he preached, in one form or another, for forty years: Christ stood in the sinner’s place and bore the sinner’s punishment. The theologians call it penal substitution. Spurgeon usually called it simply the substitution, and he regarded it as the beating heart of the gospel. Take it away, he believed, and nothing was left worth preaching.

The question that tormented him

In All of Grace Spurgeon describes the years before his conversion, and the question that kept him from peace was not a question about his feelings. It was a question about the justice of God. He knew himself guilty. He believed God ought to punish sin. And he could not see how a just God could forgive him without ceasing to be just. He did not want to be forgiven unjustly. He wanted to know how God could be both just and merciful at once.

To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus. ROMANS 3:26

The answer, when it came, came as a revelation. He saw that the Son of God had taken the place of His people, and borne in His own body the penalty their sins deserved. God did not lower the standard or blunt the sword. He turned it on Himself, in the person of His Son. What gave the doctrine its comfort, for Spurgeon, was that the sin-bearing is finished. Christ bore our sins on the tree; He bears them now no more. fields.body_html:
But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness; but unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:23–24

Spurgeon preached on almost every book of the Bible and on thousands of texts. He preached on Leviticus and on the Song of Solomon, on the ravens and the farmer’s plough, on providence, prayer, judgement and heaven. And yet his hearers agreed that he always seemed to end in the same place. Whatever road he set out on, it brought him to Calvary. This was not an accident of temperament. It was a settled conviction about what preaching is for, and indeed about what the Christian life is for.

One string on the harp

In a communion address later gathered in Till He Come, Spurgeon speaks as a preacher to other believers about the joy of praising Christ. If preachers had nothing to do but exalt their Lord — no discipline to exercise, no errors to fight, no doubts to answer — they would have heavenly work. “For my part,” he says, “I wish I could be bound over to play only upon this one string.” He admits he cannot. A pastor must deal with sin and error and sorrow. But he wanted everything else to be tuned to that one string.

For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:2

He took Paul at his word. The apostle was not refusing to teach anything else; his letters range over marriage, money, meat offered to idols and the resurrection of the body. He was refusing to let anything else become the centre. Every subject was to be handled in relation to the crucified Christ, and nothing was to be taught that would make Him less necessary.

Spurgeon is remembered for telling young preachers that, just as every village in England has a road that leads eventually to London, so from every text in Scripture there is a road to Christ, and the preacher’s business is to find it. Whether or not the words are exactly his, the conviction certainly is, and it shaped every sermon he preached.

What it means to preach Christ

In an early sermon on 1 Corinthians 1:23–24, Christ Crucified, preached at Exeter Hall in the first years of his London ministry, he sets out what he thinks preaching Christ does and does not mean. It does not mean giving people a weekly dose of philosophy while neglecting the Bible. It does not mean a religion that is all mist and haze, without definite truths. And he offers a simple test: “I take it that man does not preach Christ and him crucified, who can get through a sermon without mentioning Christ’s name once.”

That is a searching test, and not only for preachers. It is entirely possible to talk a great deal about religion — about morality, family, church life, the state of the nation — and hardly mention Christ at all. Spurgeon thought that such religion, however respectable, was not the gospel.

Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved. ACTS 4:12

He also insisted that preaching Christ meant preaching the Holy Spirit’s work, the sovereignty of grace, justification by faith and the substitution of Christ. For Spurgeon, Christ was not a sentiment but a Person with a work, and the work had definite content. A Christ without the cross, or a cross without the atonement, was not the Christ of the apostles.

Why Christ is precious

The preaching of Christ was not for Spurgeon a professional duty. It was the overflow of love. Some years into his London ministry he preached on 1 Peter 2:7, Unto you therefore which believe he is precious, and he began by telling the congregation that this was the text on which he had preached his very first sermon, as a lad of sixteen in a cottage near Cambridge. He had chosen it, he said, because he could not have spoken on anything else; Christ was precious to his soul. And now, years later and famous, he told them that Christ was more precious to him than ever.

Unto you therefore which believe he is precious. 1 PETER 2:7

This is the secret of his Christ-centred preaching. You speak most of what you love most. In a passage gathered in Gleanings Among the Sheaves he confesses that he never tires of the theme: “The monotony of Christ is sweet variety.” He adds that when believers complain of cold love to the Saviour, the answer is not to try to work up feelings but to spend more time in His presence, thinking of what He has done, until love grows in proportion as His love is realised.

We love him, because he first loved us. 1 JOHN 4:19

A stumbling-block still

Spurgeon never imagined that preaching Christ would make a preacher popular. The text itself says that Christ crucified is a stumbling-block and foolishness. In the sermon Christ Crucified he applies this with some force to his own hearers. There were religious people then, as now, who loved the outward forms of church life and would listen gladly to sermons about good conduct, but bristled at being told they needed a new heart and a crucified Saviour. There were clever people who wanted a more sophisticated message. Both, he said, stumble at the same place.

For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:18

The reader should know that some of the language of that early sermon, particularly about the Jewish people, is harsher than a Christian today would or should use. Spurgeon longed for the conversion of the Jewish people, but the rhetoric of the Victorian pulpit could be coarse. It is also true that his determination to find Christ everywhere sometimes led him into readings of the Old Testament, and especially of the Song of Solomon, that stretch the text further than careful interpretation allows. The instinct is right; the Scriptures do testify of Christ. The method needs the discipline of the plain sense.

Christ in the ordinary Christian’s mouth

The same communion address that speaks of the one string ends with a word for those who are not preachers. They cannot do better, Spurgeon says, than speak much of Jesus whenever opportunity allows, and make Him the theme of their conversation. People talk a great deal about ministers, and churches, and the state of religion. It would be better, he thought, if they talked more of Christ.

They that feared the Lord spake often one to another. MALACHI 3:16

That is a test anyone can apply. Listen to the conversation after church next Sunday, or to your own conversation with Christian friends. How much of it is about Him?

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Apply Spurgeon’s test to the last sermon you heard, the last Bible study you led, or the last spiritual conversation you had: was Christ named?

2. Choose a passage of the Old Testament you know well, and ask honestly and carefully how it leads to Christ, without forcing it.

3. If your love for Christ feels cold, do not try to manufacture feeling. Spend twenty minutes this week reading a Gospel account of the crucifixion slowly.

4. Notice what you most often talk about with other Christians. Deliberately turn one conversation this week towards Christ Himself.

5. Ask God to show you whether any part of your religion would continue unchanged if Christ were removed from it.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You are precious to those who believe, and I confess that I have often found other things more interesting than You.
I have talked about church and ministry and morality, and left You out of the conversation.
Tune my whole life to one string. Let every road I travel lead me back to Your cross.
Make me glad to be called foolish for Your sake, and let the preaching of the cross be to me the power of God. Amen.

fields.title: Free Grace
fields.body_html:
Not for your sakes do I this, saith the Lord God, be it known unto you: be ashamed and confounded for your own ways, O house of Israel. EZEKIEL 36:32

Spurgeon was a Calvinist, and he never hid it. He grew up on the Puritans, he preached the doctrines of grace from his first pulpit to his last, and in his early sermon Christ Crucified he went so far as to say that it was a nickname to call these truths Calvinism, since in his view they were simply the gospel. Many readers will not share all his convictions here. But before deciding what to make of his Calvinism, it is worth seeing what it was for. It was not a system for sorting people. It was a doxology. Its whole purpose was to take every scrap of credit for salvation away from man and give it to God.

Two sins bred in the bone

He opens his sermon Free Grace, on a text from Ezekiel, with a diagnosis. There are two sins of man, he says, that are bred in the bone and continually come out in the flesh: self-dependence and self-exaltation. Even the holiest Christians feel the pull of both. We want to contribute something to our salvation, and then we want to be admired for it. Against both, Scripture keeps reminding us of a single truth. Salvation, Spurgeon says, “is God’s work from first to last, and is not of man, neither by man.”

Salvation is of the Lord. JONAH 2:9

He illustrates this from Abraham. God promised him a son, and Abraham believed; but when the promise was slow in coming, he took Hagar, and Ishmael was born. Abraham thought he was helping God keep His word. Instead he brought sorrow into his house. Spurgeon thought many Christians do the same. Instead of looking to grace alone, they set to work to assist Omnipotence, and they only sink themselves deeper in the mire.

The reason is in God

The heart of the sermon is an uncomfortable question. Why is one person saved and another not? Spurgeon’s answer is that the reason lies not in the person saved but in the heart of God. There was nothing in any of us to recommend us. All were alike lost, all without a claim on mercy. God’s choice was, as far as anything in us is concerned, without cause. It was the effect of His sovereign love.

According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love. EPHESIANS 1:4

He knew perfectly well how this lands on the natural mind. People are happy, he observes, to accept that God passed by the fallen angels and saved men; nobody complains about that. “Every man approves of Calvinism till he feels that he is the loser by it.” It is only when the doctrine touches us personally that we object. Spurgeon did not think the objection answered the Scripture.

So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. ROMANS 9:16

Why he found it joyful

What is striking about Spurgeon’s preaching of election is its tone. He did not preach it grimly or defensively. He preached it with delight. In Free Grace he tells his congregation that when he was meditating on the text the day before, it filled him with transport and joy. He looked back on his own life — piously brought up, and in rebellion against it all, his mother’s tears shed in vain and his father’s warnings lost on him — and he found himself saved anyway, by grace. If it had been by merit, he says, “I had never been saved.”

That is the key to his Calvinism. It was not first a theory about other people. It was the explanation of his own conversion. When he asked himself why he had believed, he could find no answer in himself. He had heard the same gospel for years and rejected it. Something had to be done in him that he could not do for himself. He concluded that God had done it, and that God had meant to do it, and that it was all of grace.

For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? 1 CORINTHIANS 4:7

The rock that does not move

For Spurgeon, sovereign grace was also the ground of the believer’s security. The sermon that stands first in the printed series of his sermons, The Immutability of God, preached in January 1855, begins with the words of Malachi: I am the Lord, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed. fields.body_html:
And the lord said unto the servant, Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled. LUKE 14:23

If the last chapter showed Spurgeon as a Calvinist, this one shows him as an evangelist, and the two cannot be separated without misunderstanding him. The same man who believed that God had chosen His people before the foundation of the world stood up week after week and pleaded with every person in front of him to come to Christ at once. He did not think these were rival truths needing to be balanced. He thought both were in the Bible, and that his business was to preach both with all his strength.

No time for an introduction

His sermon Compel Them to Come In, preached in the Surrey Gardens Music Hall in 1858, opens without the usual preliminaries. He says he feels in such haste to obey the command in the text that he cannot wait for an introduction, and must set about his business at once. And his business is to lay hold of the people in front of him.

He tells them plainly that they have fallen, in Adam and in themselves, and that a just God must punish sin. Then he tells them that God has provided a way of mercy through His Son, who died the just for the unjust, and that the way is simple: whosoever believes in the Lord Jesus Christ shall be saved. All God asks, he says, is that they look at His dying Son and trust Him — and even that, God gives.

The Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely. REVELATION 22:17

What follows is one of the most urgent sermons in the English language. He pleads, he argues, he weeps. He imagines standing by the coffin of a hearer who rejected Christ, and hearing the dead man reproach him: you amused me, you preached to me, but you did not plead with me. He cannot bear the thought. He tells them that he would be destitute of all humanity if he saw someone about to drink poison and did not dash the cup away.

I must do it

At the height of the sermon he pauses to answer an objection he knew would come. There were Calvinists in his day, usually called hyper-Calvinists, who taught that it was wrong to urge the unconverted to believe, since only the elect could, and to press the invitation on everyone was to imply a power in fallen man that he did not have. Spurgeon had no patience with this. “Some hyper-calvinist would tell me I am wrong in so doing,” he says. “I cannot help it. I must do it.” He would not make full proof of his ministry, he tells them, unless he entreated them with many tears to be saved.

Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ’s stead, be ye reconciled to God. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:20

He thought this pleading was not in spite of his theology but because of the Bible. God Himself commands all men everywhere to repent. The Lord wept over Jerusalem. Paul could wish himself accursed for his kinsmen’s sake. The preacher who does not plead, however orthodox his doctrine, has not understood the heart of the God he preaches.

Say unto them, As I live, saith the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel? EZEKIEL 33:11

The Spirit holds the key

Yet the same sermon ends in a way no Arminian preacher would have ended it. Having pleaded with every argument he had, Spurgeon turns from his hearers to God. He has preached the gospel earnestly; now he appeals to the Spirit. “I cannot compel you,” he says, “but thou O Spirit of God who hast the key of the heart, thou canst compel.” He points out that the Christ who stands at the door and knocks in Revelation is the same Christ who holds the key of David. If knocking does not prevail, He can open.

Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me. REVELATION 3:20

This is how Spurgeon held the two truths together in practice. He did everything a man could do, as if everything depended on him. Then he threw the whole matter into his Master’s hands, confident that God would not let His word return void. The sovereignty of God did not make him passive. It made him bold, because it assured him that his pleading was not in vain.

Calvinism and Calvary

He was also honest about the danger on his own side. In a sermon on The Sweet Uses of Adversity he confesses to his congregation that ministers, himself included, can dim the lustre of grace. “Often am I afraid lest I should prefer Calvinism to Calvary,” he says, and he fears putting the sinner’s sense of need like a hedge around the cross, keeping poor sinners from coming near. It is a remarkable admission from a man so committed to his system. He knew that doctrine could become a wall instead of a door.

Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. JOHN 6:37

His sermon The Sinner’s Friend makes the same point from the side of Christ. The Pharisees called Jesus a friend of publicans and sinners as an insult, and the insult became the glory of His name. The Saviour is not waiting for sinners to become respectable. He seeks them where they are.

What this asks of us

Most Christians today do not preach to thousands. But the question Spurgeon’s sermon puts is not only for preachers. Do we believe that the people we know are really lost without Christ? Do we believe He really receives anyone who comes? And if we believe both, why are we so rarely in earnest?

The reader who does not share Spurgeon’s Calvinism will still find him a searching guide here, perhaps more searching than many preachers who do. And the reader who does share it will find in him a standing rebuke to any theology that makes evangelism optional.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read Luke 14:15–24 and notice who is invited, who refuses, and who finally comes in.

2. Ask honestly whether your theology — whatever it is — has ever become an excuse for not speaking to someone about Christ.

3. Think of one person you know who is far from God. Pray for them by name every day this week, asking the Spirit who holds the key to open their heart.

4. Look for one natural opportunity to invite someone, warmly and without pressure, to hear the gospel.

5. If you tend to plead but not to pray, or to pray but not to plead, ask God to give you both.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, Friend of sinners, You sent Your servants into the highways and hedges, and You found me there.
Forgive me for how rarely I plead with anyone. I have been more afraid of embarrassment than of their eternal loss.
Give me earnestness to beseech, and humility to know that I cannot compel. You hold the key of the heart.
Fill Your house, Lord, and let some of those I love be among the guests. Amen.

fields.title: Faith Very Simple
fields.body_html:
Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved. ACTS 16:31

Spurgeon spent his life explaining faith to people who thought it must be harder than it is. He had been one of them. For years before his conversion he waited for something mysterious and difficult to happen inside him, and when it came, it was as simple as looking. He never forgot the surprise, and he wrote two small books, All of Grace and Around the Wicket Gate, largely to spare others the years he had wasted.

Hard because it is easy

In Around the Wicket Gate he gives a whole chapter the title Faith very Simple, and he opens it with a paradox. To many people faith seems a hard thing. “The truth is,” he says, “it is only hard because it is easy.” He points to Naaman, who was offended at being told to wash in the Jordan. If the prophet had bid him do some great thing, he would have done it gladly. It was the simplicity of the remedy that he could not stomach.

My father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? how much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean? 2 KINGS 5:13

People expect salvation to be the reward of some mysterious experience, Spurgeon says, and so they are bewildered when they find it offered for the taking. The trouble is not that they cannot understand. It is that they do not believe God means what He says.

He tells a story of a Sunday-school teacher who, trying to explain faith, held out his watch to each boy in turn and offered it to him. One after another they hesitated or politely declined, suspecting a trick. At last a younger boy simply said thank you and put it in his pocket. The others were horrified to discover that the offer had been real. Each of them had a theory, and none of them had the watch. Spurgeon’s point is obvious and piercing. God is not playing with us when He offers His Son.

Knowledge, belief and trust

In All of Grace he gives a more careful account. Faith, he says, is made up of three things: knowledge, belief and trust. You must first know what the gospel says, for you cannot believe what you have never heard. You must then believe it to be true — that Christ is who He is said to be, and will do what He has promised. And then comes the decisive step. You must trust Him, resting your own soul on Him.

So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. ROMANS 10:17

“Trust is the lifeblood of faith,” Spurgeon writes; “there is no saving faith without it.” He borrows a word from the Puritans, recumbency, meaning to lean on something. “Lean with all your weight upon Christ,” he says, and then corrects himself to something stronger still: fall at full length and lie on the Rock of Ages.

This is a helpful correction to two opposite mistakes. Some treat faith as mere agreement with a creed; they believe the facts and never commit themselves. Others treat faith as a leap in the dark with no content at all. Spurgeon’s faith is neither. It begins with knowledge, it rests on facts, and it ends in personal trust in a Person.

For I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day. 2 TIMOTHY 1:12

The hand that takes

Why did God choose faith, rather than love or patience or obedience, as the way of receiving salvation? Spurgeon answers modestly in All of Grace: as far as we can tell, it is because faith is fitted to receive. When you give a poor man money, you put it in his hand, because the hand is made for taking. Faith is the hand of the soul.

He puts it in a homely picture. A child reaches out for an apple its father holds out. “The child’s hand does not make the apple, nor improve the apple, nor deserve the apple; it only takes it.” That is what faith does with salvation. It adds nothing, earns nothing, and so leaves all the glory to God.

Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace. ROMANS 4:16

This is why Spurgeon insisted that weak faith saves as surely as strong faith. The power is not in the hand but in what it holds. A trembling hand that grips a sure rope is as safe as a steady one. Many anxious believers torment themselves by examining their faith, wondering if it is strong enough or real enough. Spurgeon told them to stop examining their hand and look at Christ.

The shortest way to believe

Some people say they want to believe but cannot. Spurgeon was practical with them. In All of Grace he says that a great deal of nonsense is talked about this, and that common sense is needed in religion as anywhere else. “The shortest way to believe is to believe.” If truth is set before you, believe it because it is true.

If there are real difficulties, he says, take them to God in prayer and ask the Holy Spirit to make them plain. Hear the gospel often. Think about the Person of Christ. Consider the testimony of those who have trusted Him. But do not wait for a feeling to come before you obey the command.

Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. MARK 9:24

Simple, but not shallow

A word of caution belongs here. Spurgeon’s insistence on simplicity can be misheard as if faith were a quick decision, a form of words, or a raised hand at the end of a meeting. He meant nothing of the kind. He believed faith to be the gift of God, worked in the heart by the Holy Spirit, and always joined to repentance. He expected it to show itself in a changed life. What he insisted was that none of those things is a condition to be met before coming. They come with faith and after it, not as its price.

He also warned against the opposite error: making faith so complicated, so hedged with qualifications and inward tests, that nobody dares to exercise it. That is the error he saw in much of the preaching he heard as a boy, and he spent his life undoing it.

The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart: that is, the word of faith, which we preach. ROMANS 10:8
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask whether you, like Naaman, have wanted salvation to require something greater than trust. What would you rather do than simply believe?

2. Write down what you know of Christ, what you believe about Him, and where you have actually trusted Him. Which of the three is weakest?

3. Stop examining the strength of your faith this week. Each time you are tempted to, turn instead to a promise of Christ and rest on it.

4. If you have been waiting to feel something before you believe, take Spurgeon’s counsel: the shortest way to believe is to believe. Do it now, in prayer.

5. Explain the child and the apple to someone else. Nothing fixes a truth in the mind like teaching it.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You hold out salvation as a gift, and I have hesitated as if You were not in earnest.
I have looked for something great to do, and stumbled at the simplicity of trusting You.
I lean my whole weight on You now. I have nothing to add and nothing to pay. I take what You give.
When my hand trembles, let me look at what it holds, and not at the hand. Lord, I believe; help Thou mine unbelief. Amen.

If the prophet had bid him do some great thing, he would have done it gladly. It was the simplicity of the remedy that he could not stomach. He also warned against the opposite error: making faith so complicated, so hedged with qualifications and inward tests, that nobody dares to exercise it. That is the error he saw in much of the preaching he heard as a boy, and he spent his life undoing it. The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart: that is, the word of faith, which we preach. ROMANS 10:8 FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Ask whether you, like Naaman, have wanted salvation to require something greater than trust. What would you rather do than simply believe? 2. Write down what you know of Christ, what you believe about Him, and where you have actually trusted Him. Which of the three is weakest? 3. Stop examining the strength of your faith this week. Each time you are tempted to, turn instead to a promise of Christ and rest on it. 4. If you have been waiting to feel something before you believe, take Spurgeon’s counsel: the shortest way to believe is to believe. Do it now, in prayer. 5. Explain the child and the apple to someone else. Nothing fixes a truth in the mind like teaching it. A PRAYER Lord Jesus, You hold out salvation as a gift, and I have hesitated as if You were not in earnest. I have looked for something great to do, and stumbled at the simplicity of trusting You. I lean my whole weight on You now. I have nothing to add and nothing to pay. I take what You give. When my hand trembles, let me look at what it holds, and not at the hand. Lord, I believe; help Thou mine unbelief. Amen.

fields.title: Repentance Must Go with Forgiveness
fields.body_html:
Him hath God exalted with his right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins. ACTS 5:31

A preacher who says as often as Spurgeon did that salvation is simply a look will be asked, sooner or later, what has become of repentance. Spurgeon heard the question all his life, and took it seriously. In the later chapters of All of Grace, having spent chapter after chapter pressing the free offer on the reader, he stops to give two chapters to it, under the plain title Repentance Must Go with Forgiveness. His answer is not a condition added to grace. It is another gift of the same grace, from the same pierced hand.

Riveted together

He begins from his text in Acts. The risen Christ is exalted to give two things, repentance and forgiveness, and Spurgeon will not allow them to be separated. “Repentance and forgiveness are riveted together by the eternal purpose of God.” What God has joined, he says, let no man put asunder.

And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem. LUKE 24:47

He gives two reasons why it must be so. The first is the holiness of God. A pardon offered to someone who loves his sin and means to go on in it would be a licence for iniquity. No rebel can expect the King to pardon his treason while he remains in open revolt. The second reason is less obvious and more beautiful: the completeness of mercy. A mercy that forgave the sin and left the sinner in it would be, as he puts it, lame on one foot and withered in one hand. What use is it to bring a man out of the grave if you leave him dead? To be pronounced clean and still have the leprosy on one’s brow would be a mockery of mercy.

Would you, he asks the reader, be content to be forgiven and left as worldly as before? The quickened soul is more afraid of sin itself than of its punishment.

Two handles of one plough

The heart of the chapter is his account of how repentance and faith belong together. They are not stages, one finished before the other begins. “Repentance is the inseparable companion of faith.” All the while we walk by faith, he says, “the tear of repentance glitters in the eye of faith.” Faith that has no sorrow for sin in it is not true faith, and sorrow for sin that does not look to Jesus is not true repentance.

For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death. 2 CORINTHIANS 7:10

He has a string of pictures for the bond. They are the Jachin and Boaz of a saving experience, the two pillars at the door of Solomon’s temple, and nobody comes to God aright except between them. “Faith and repentance are but two spokes in the same wheel, two handles of the same plough.” He quotes a description he admired, that repentance is a heart broken for sin, and from sin — grieved over what it has done, and turned away from doing it.

This has a practical edge. Repentance, Spurgeon insists, is not a thing of days and weeks, a penance to be got through as quickly as possible and then left behind. It is “the grace of a lifetime, like faith itself.” The young Christian repents and so does the old one, and the older one often repents more deeply, because he has seen more of the love he has sinned against.

The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise. PSALM 51:17

Pardon melts the heart

Here Spurgeon makes a move that many readers find surprising. We tend to assume that repentance comes first and earns forgiveness: we grieve, and so God pardons. He will not have it. “Do not regard your repentance as the cause of your remission, but as the companion of it.” Indeed, he says, forgiveness leads to repentance as much as the reverse. He quotes a verse of Joseph Hart’s hymn to the effect that law and terrors only harden, while a sense of blood-bought pardon dissolves a heart of stone.

Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance? ROMANS 2:4

It follows that the surest way to repent is not to stare into your own heart but to look at the cross. “Do not sit down and try to pump up repentance from the dry well of corrupt nature,” he writes. Nobody can force his soul into a penitent frame. The more you try to produce the right emotions, the more you will be disappointed. But if you think of Jesus dying for you, sorrow for sin will come of itself. He points to Peter in the high priest’s courtyard. The Lord turned and looked on him, and that look did what no argument could.

And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord … And Peter went out, and wept bitterly. LUKE 22:61–62

We repent ourselves; nobody can do it for us. But behind our turning, Spurgeon says, is the Spirit, who shows us what sin is and makes it loathsome. And the exalted Christ uses everything else as well — conscience, Scripture, preaching, the prayers of friends and the hard providences of life. “The Lord’s mercy often rides to the door of our hearts on the black horse of affliction.”

Hope for the hardest

Spurgeon lingers with evident delight on one word of his text: Christ is exalted to give repentance to Israel — to the very people who had cried out for His crucifixion. If He could give repentance to them, there is no heart He cannot soften. The Lord, Spurgeon says, can turn lions into lambs and ravens into doves.

The Lord is … longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. 2 PETER 3:9

That is the note on which he ends, and it is a gospel note. The reader who feels he cannot repent is not told to try harder. He is told to ask. Repentance is as much a gift of grace as the atonement itself, and the risen Christ is ready to give it now.

A word of care

Two cautions are worth adding. The first is that Spurgeon’s insistence that repentance is lifelong can, in a tender conscience, curdle into a habit of endless self-examination that never rests in pardon. The bitterness of repentance and the sweetness of pardon, he says, blend in every gracious life and make up an incomparable happiness. Repentance that never tastes the pardon has gone wrong.

The second is that Christians have long differed over the order of these things, and some traditions speak of repentance as preparing the way for faith. Spurgeon was not greatly interested in drawing a timetable. His point is simpler and almost every believer can own it: repentance is not a price paid to God but a gift received from Christ, and it grows, like faith, by looking at Him.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask whether you have wanted forgiveness without wanting to be free of the sin itself. Tell God honestly which one you have been asking for.

2. If you feel unable to repent, stop trying to manufacture feeling. Read the account of the crucifixion in Luke 23 slowly, and let Christ look at you.

3. Name one sin you have confessed many times but never turned from. Decide on one concrete step away from it this week.

4. Notice whether your repentance ever reaches rest in pardon. If it does not, read 1 John 1:9 aloud and believe it.

5. Think of someone you have written off as too hard to change. Pray for them by name, remembering that Christ gave repentance to those who crucified Him.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, exalted Prince and Saviour, You give repentance and forgiveness, and I need both.
I have wanted to be pardoned more than I have wanted to be made holy. Break my heart for sin, and from sin.
I cannot pump repentance out of a dry well. Look on me as You looked on Peter, and let me weep and be healed.
Keep the tear of repentance and the light of pardon together in my eyes, all my life long. Amen.

fields.title: I Change Not
fields.body_html:
For I am the Lord, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed. MALACHI 3:6

Spurgeon was twenty when he preached The Immutability of God, one of the first sermons of his London ministry and the one that opens the long series of his printed sermons. It is a young man’s sermon, full of energy and not without overstatement. But it shows where his confidence came from. Before he spoke of promises to be pleaded or of saints who would persevere, he wanted his hearers to look at God Himself — and in particular at the fact that He does not change.

The proper study of a Christian

He begins by adapting a famous line of Alexander Pope. It has been said that the proper study of mankind is man. Spurgeon does not quarrel with it, but he sets another beside it: “the proper study of a Christian is the Godhead.” No other subject, he says, so humbles the mind, because our plumb-line cannot sound its depth. No other so enlarges it. And no other so comforts it. “Would you lose your sorrows? Would you drown your cares? Then go, plunge yourself in the Godhead’s deepest sea.”

Thus saith the Lord, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom … But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me. JEREMIAH 9:23–24

That is worth pausing over, because it is not how most of us look for comfort. When we are troubled we tend to think about the trouble, or about ourselves. Spurgeon’s counsel is to think about God — not as an escape from the trouble, but because the character of God is the one fixed point from which the trouble can be measured.

Semper idem

The body of the sermon sets out what it means for God not to change. He does not change in His essence. Everything created is in flux: mountains shed their snow, the sea is drawn up into the clouds, the atoms of our bodies are replaced year by year. But God is spirit, and “there are no furrows on his eternal brow.” Even the incarnation, Spurgeon notes carefully, did not alter the divine nature; the Godhead was the same in the manger as when it stretched out the heavens.

They shall perish, but thou shalt endure: yea, all of them shall wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed: but thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end. PSALM 102:26–27

Nor does He change in His attributes. His power, wisdom, justice and truth are what they always were, and so is His love, which, Spurgeon says, “stands like a granite rock, unmoved by the hurricanes of our iniquity.” “Take any one attribute of God,” he says, “and I will write semper idem on it” — always the same.

Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning. JAMES 1:17

He does not change in His plans either. A man may begin to build and find he cannot finish. God has boundless resources, perfect wisdom and endless life; He has no reason to alter His purpose and nothing that could force Him to. Spurgeon draws the personal conclusion with characteristic directness: if God has told me that His plan is to save me, then I am safe.

The bank that never fails

The most useful part of the sermon, for ordinary believers, is what he says about the promises. If any promise of God could be altered, he says, we would do better not to talk of them at all. “If I thought that the notes of the bank of England could not be cashed next week, I should decline to take them.” It is the same picture he would use thirty years later in The Cheque Book of the Bank of Faith, and it rests on the same foundation. The promises are worth pleading only because the One who made them does not change.

That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us. HEBREWS 6:18

He then deals tenderly with a common experience. A promise that was sweet yesterday tastes of nothing today, and the believer wonders whether it has failed. Not at all, Spurgeon says: “You changed; that is where the matter lies.” The honey is still in the comb. And when a believer feels his house of hope blown down, it was only the little hut of wood, hay and stubble he had built for himself. “You have been shaken on the rock, not the rock under you.”

Not consumed

The last part of the sermon turns to the second half of the text. Why are the sons of Jacob not consumed? Not because they are good. Spurgeon is frank that God’s family is the most troublesome family in the world — unbelieving, ungrateful, forgetful and stiffnecked — and that any earthly father would long ago have given up. They survive because God’s love to them never rested on anything in them. “Since their good works did not win his affection, bad works cannot sever that affection.”

It is of the Lord’s mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness. LAMENTATIONS 3:22–23

He speaks, too, of times in his own life when temptation had dragged him to the edge of some great sin and a strong arm had pulled him back. He was still standing, he says, only because the Lord does not change. And he closes with a sentence that sums up the whole sermon: “Remember God is the same, whatever is removed.” Friends may cool, ministers may be taken away, health and property may go. There is one heart that never alters.

Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. HEBREWS 13:8

Where he needs care

This early sermon has faults the older Spurgeon would have recognised. His treatment of the unchanging threatenings of God is fierce, and the lurid lines about the lost reading their sentence in letters of fire for a million ages are harder than the text requires. The warning is real — Scripture is plain that he that believeth not shall be damned (Mark 16:16) — but it is better spoken with tears than with relish.

His handling of Hezekiah also needs a word. To show that God did not change His mind when He added fifteen years to the king’s life, Spurgeon suggests that Isaiah had simply not finished his sentence before he left the room. That is an ingenious guess, not what the text says. Scripture does speak of God relenting when people turn (Jonah 3:10), and the better answer is that an unchanging God has always purposed to answer prayer and to show mercy to the penitent. His constancy is not the stillness of a stone but the faithfulness of a Person. Spurgeon’s own life of prayer shows that he believed exactly this.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. The next time you are anxious, spend five minutes thinking not about the problem but about one attribute of God. Write semper idem beside it.

2. Recall a promise that once meant much to you and now feels flat. Ask whether the promise has changed, or you have.

3. List the things in your life that you fear losing. Beside the list, write Malachi 3:6.

4. Read Lamentations 3:19–26, and thank God specifically for one mercy that was new this morning.

5. If you have been presuming on God’s patience with a known sin, remember that His warnings are as unchanging as His promises, and turn today.

A PRAYER
Unchanging God, everything I lean on moves: my health, my friends, my feelings, even my faith.
But You are the same, and Your years have no end. There are no furrows on Your brow and no shadow of turning in Your heart.
When Your promises taste of nothing, teach me that it is I who have changed, and bring me back to the rock.
I am not consumed only because Your compassions fail not. Great is Your faithfulness, through Jesus Christ, who is the same for ever. Amen.

There is one heart that never alters. Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. His treatment of the unchanging threatenings of God is fierce, and the lurid lines about the lost reading their sentence in letters of fire for a million ages are harder than the text requires. The warning is real — Scripture is plain that he that believeth not shall be damned (Mark 16:16) — but it is better spoken with tears than with relish. His handling of Hezekiah also needs a word.
