That is an ingenious guess, not what the text says. Scripture does speak of God relenting when people turn (Jonah 3:10), and the better answer is that an unchanging God has always purposed to answer prayer and to show mercy to the penitent. His constancy is not the stillness of a stone but the faithfulness of a Person. Spurgeon’s own life of prayer shows that he believed exactly this. FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. The next time you are anxious, spend five minutes thinking not about the problem but about one attribute of God. Write semper idem beside it. 2. Recall a promise that once meant much to you and now feels flat. Ask whether the promise has changed, or you have. 3. List the things in your life that you fear losing. Beside the list, write Malachi 3:6. 4. Read Lamentations 3:19–26, and thank God specifically for one mercy that was new this morning. 5. If you have been presuming on God’s patience with a known sin, remember that His warnings are as unchanging as His promises, and turn today. There are no furrows on Your brow and no shadow of turning in Your heart. When Your promises taste of nothing, teach me that it is I who have changed, and bring me back to the rock. I am not consumed only because Your compassions fail not. Great is Your faithfulness, through Jesus Christ, who is the same for ever. Amen.

fields.body_html:
Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature. 2 PETER 1:4

In the late 1880s, in the middle of the hardest years of his life, Spurgeon published a small book of daily readings. Each day has a single promise of Scripture and a short page of comment. He called it The Cheque Book of the Bank of Faith, and in the preface he explained the title with a picture any Victorian businessman would understand. It is one of the most useful pictures he ever drew, and it sums up his whole approach to the promises of God.

A cheque, not a picture

A promise from God, he says, may be compared to a cheque made payable to order. It is given to the believer to bestow some good thing on him. And then comes the sentence on which everything turns: “It is not meant that he should read it over comfortably, and then have done with it.” Nobody frames a cheque and hangs it on the wall to admire. You take it to the bank.

So with the promises. The believer must first endorse the cheque with his own name, by receiving the promise personally as true for him. Then he must present it at the counter, by pleading it in prayer and expecting God to honour it. If the date has arrived, he receives the payment at once. If the cheque is post-dated, he must wait; but he may count it as good as money in the meantime, because the bank is sure to pay when the day comes.

For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us. 2 CORINTHIANS 1:20

Some people, he observes, never endorse the cheque, and so receive nothing. Others never present it. The fault is not in the promise but in their failure to deal with it in a plain, businesslike way. And he states his confidence in words that could stand over the whole book: “God has given no pledge which He will not redeem, and encouraged no hope which He will not fulfill.”

Written in deep water

What gives the Cheque Book its authority is the circumstances in which it was written. Spurgeon says in the preface that he began the daily portions while wading in the surf of controversy — the Down-Grade struggle that cost him so many friends. Since then, he writes, he had been cast into waters to swim in. Mental depression had been followed by sharp bodily pain, and both by bereavement and by illness in one dear to him as life. He mentions it, he says, not to gain sympathy but so that the reader will know he is writing from experience. “I am no dry-land sailor.”

He adds that the promises had never been so precious to him as then, and that some of them he had never understood until that season. He had not reached the date on which they matured. That is a striking admission from a man who had preached for more than thirty years. There are promises which cannot be cashed until the trouble for which they were written arrives.

This is my comfort in my affliction: for thy word hath quickened me. PSALM 119:50

Pleading the promise

For Spurgeon the promises were chiefly material for prayer. On one page of the Cheque Book he comments on David’s prayer in 2 Samuel 7, where the king takes what God has said and turns it back to God as a petition: Thou, O Lord God, hast spoken it. This, Spurgeon says, is a promise pleaded. We receive what God has said as surely true, and then we plead it at the throne. “We do not pray because we doubt, but because we believe.”

And now, O Lord God, the word that thou hast spoken concerning thy servant … establish it for ever, and do as thou hast said. 2 SAMUEL 7:25

This gives prayer a solid floor. Much praying is vague: we tell God what we would like and hope He agrees. Praying the promises is different. We come with His own words in our hand and ask Him to do what He has said. That is not presumption; it is taking Him seriously. Chapter thirteen follows this further.

Rich beyond telling

In a passage gathered in Gleanings Among the Sheaves, Spurgeon piles up pictures to describe the promises. They are, he says, “an inexhaustible mine of wealth.” They are an armoury full of weapons, a dispensary with a remedy for every disease, a granary like Joseph’s in Egypt, the title deeds of a heavenly estate, a jewel room where the believer may already handle the crown he will wear. The piling up is typical of his style, and it can overwhelm a modern reader. But the point beneath it is plain. Most Christians live far below their means, because they do not know what is written to their account.

Blessed be the Lord, that hath given rest unto his people Israel, according to all that he promised: there hath not failed one word of all his good promise. 1 KINGS 8:56

Reading the cheque correctly

The picture of a cheque also contains its own caution, and Spurgeon supplies part of it himself. A cheque is made out to a particular payee, for a particular sum, on a particular date. Not every promise in Scripture is addressed to every person in every situation. Some were given to Israel as a nation, some to particular individuals, some on conditions that must be met. The promise of long life to those who honour their parents is not a guarantee that every obedient child will reach old age. The cheque must be read before it is cashed.

Spurgeon was also careful about what the promises do not say. On the verse I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee, he writes in the Cheque Book: “This priceless Scripture does not promise us exemption from trouble, but it does secure us against desertion.” That sentence is a needed corrective to any gospel that treats the promises as guarantees of comfort, health or wealth. What God promises above all is Himself — His presence, His faithfulness, His grace sufficient for the day.

For he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee. HEBREWS 13:5

And some cheques are post-dated. The believer may plead a promise for years and not see it paid in this life. Spurgeon knew this. The bank is sure; the date is God’s. Faith is the confidence that the payment is certain even when it is not yet due.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Choose one promise of Scripture that speaks directly to your present situation. Write it out and put your own name on it, as an endorsement.

2. Read the promise in its context. Ask to whom it was first given, on what conditions, and whether it applies to you as it stands.

3. Turn the promise into a prayer this week, using God’s own words: Lord, You have said… do as You have said.

4. Think of a promise you once found dry that has since come alive in a hard season. Thank God for it, and share it with someone passing through something similar.

5. If you are waiting on a promise that seems post-dated, tell God honestly how long it feels, and then tell Him you trust the bank.

A PRAYER
Faithful God, You have given no pledge that You will not redeem, and I have left so many of Your promises unread and uncashed.
I have admired Your word and then walked away from it. Teach me to take You at Your word.
Where the date has come, let me receive. Where it has not, let me wait without doubting.
Above all, thank You that You have promised never to leave me nor forsake me. That promise I take today, in Jesus’ name. Amen.

fields.title: The Golden Key of Prayer
fields.body_html:
Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things, which thou knowest not. JEREMIAH 33:3

Visitors to the Metropolitan Tabernacle often wanted to know the secret of Spurgeon’s power. The story is told that he would take them down beneath the building to a room where hundreds of his people were on their knees praying for the service upstairs, and tell them that this was the power-house of the church. Whether or not every detail of the story is exact, its point is certainly his. He believed that the pulpit rested on the prayer meeting, and he preached on prayer more often and more searchingly than almost any other subject. A dozen of those sermons are gathered in the Ochorus library as Mighty Power in Prayer.

An approach of the soul

Spurgeon was careful to say what prayer is before he said how to do it. In his sermon The Throne of Grace he gives a definition that repays memorising: “True prayer is an approach of the soul by the Spirit of God to the throne of God.” It is not the saying of words, however beautiful. It is not merely having desires, however sincere. It is the movement of those desires towards God, by the help of His Spirit.

Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need. HEBREWS 4:16

That definition rules out two opposite errors. It rules out formalism, the repetition of phrases that never reach heaven. Spurgeon could be scathing about prayer meetings where people recited long, borrowed sentences. He wished that believers would talk to God as a child talks to his father, ask Him for what they wanted, and sit down. And it rules out mere emotionalism. Strong feelings are not prayer until they are carried to God.

Call, and I will answer

In The Golden Key of Prayer, on Jeremiah 33:3, he takes up the question that silences most praying before it begins: will God actually hear? His answer is emphatic. God has promised, and He cannot lie. And beyond the promise stands the cross. If God gave His Son for us, will He refuse to listen to us? “You misread Calvary,” he says, “if you think that prayer is useless.”

He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? ROMANS 8:32

He also presses the second half of the verse. God promises to show great and mighty things which we do not know. Spurgeon applied this to Christian understanding. Many truths of Scripture, he told students and Sunday-school teachers, will not open to study alone; they open to study soaked in prayer. Prayer is not a substitute for thinking, but it is the key to a door that thinking cannot unlock.

Filling the mouth with arguments

His most distinctive teaching on prayer is in Order and Argument in Prayer, on Job’s longing to find God, order his cause before Him, and fill his mouth with arguments. Spurgeon thought most praying was disorderly and argument-less. We ramble; we tell God vaguely what we would like; we do not plead.

I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments. JOB 23:4

Why argue with God at all? Not, he says, because God is reluctant or needs persuading or informing. “The arguments to be used are for our own benefit, not for his.” Searching for reasons shows that we value what we ask for. It teaches us the ground on which blessings come, which is always grace and never merit. And it stirs up fervency. He recalls that the best prayers he ever heard in the Tabernacle prayer meetings were the ones fullest of argument, where a brother pleaded for a mercy for one reason, then another, then another, until the whole meeting was on fire.

What are the arguments? God’s own attributes — His justice, His mercy, His faithfulness. His promises, which is where the last chapter left us. His great name, and the glory it would gain. Our own need and misery. The past mercies He has already shown. And above all, the blood of Christ. These are the arguments Moses used, and David, and Daniel.

O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive; O Lord, hearken and do; defer not, for thine own sake, O my God. DANIEL 9:19

He adds that the one who fills his mouth with arguments will soon have it filled with praise. “The man who has his mouth full of arguments in prayer shall soon have his mouth full of benedictions in answer to prayer.” And even apart from the answer, he says, prayer is itself a blessing. To pray is to enter the treasure-house of God.

The church on its knees

Spurgeon did not think of prayer only as a private exercise. He thought the prayer meeting was the most important meeting of the church, and he said so constantly. In one of these sermons he calls it “an invaluable institution, ministering strength to all other meetings and agencies,” and he rebukes those who stay away on any small excuse. He believed that the blessing on the preaching came from the praying, and he was not being modest. He meant it as a plain statement of cause and effect.

These all continued with one accord in prayer and supplication. ACTS 1:14

It is worth pausing on how rare that conviction has become. Most churches today put a great deal of energy into the Sunday service and comparatively little into the gathering for prayer. Spurgeon would have regarded that as a church cutting off its own supply.

The prayers of seekers

One more feature of his teaching deserves notice, because it set him against some Calvinists of his time. In his sermon The Ravens’ Cry he encourages the unconverted to pray. If God hears the young ravens when they cry, will He not hear a sinner crying for mercy? He recalls telling children in an ultra-Calvinist chapel that he had prayed for ordinary mercies long before his conversion and that God had heard him — and being surrounded afterwards by men calling it rank Arminianism. He was unmoved. To the anxious hearer puzzling over whether his cry is natural or spiritual, his counsel is simple: whichever it is, “still continue to seek the Lord!”

It is fair to add that Spurgeon’s language about prevailing prayer can sound, if lifted out of context, as though persistence could bend God’s will. He did not believe that. Prayer, for him, was the appointed means by which God accomplishes what He has purposed. We do not change His mind; we are changed, and His purposes are fulfilled through our asking.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Test your last prayer against Spurgeon’s definition. Was it an approach of the soul to God, or only words and wishes?

2. Choose one thing you are praying for. Write down at least four arguments from Scripture — God’s character, His promises, His glory, past mercies — and plead them.

3. If you have been praying in borrowed phrases, try this week to speak to God as a child speaks to a father: plainly, and then stop.

4. If your church has a prayer meeting you rarely attend, go to the next one. If it has none, ask whether you could help begin one.

5. Before studying Scripture this week, pray Jeremiah 33:3 and ask God to show you what you do not yet know.

A PRAYER
Father, You have said, Call unto Me, and I will answer thee, and I have called so seldom and so vaguely.
I come now by Your Spirit to Your throne, which is a throne of grace. I bring no merit, only Your promises and the blood of Your Son.
Teach me to order my cause before You and to fill my mouth with arguments, not because You are unwilling, but because I need to learn how much I need You.
Make Your church a praying church, and begin with me. Amen.

fields.title: The Word and the Spirit
fields.body_html:
Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts. ZECHARIAH 4:6

Spurgeon was the most gifted preacher of his century, and he knew it. He had a voice that could reach the back of a vast hall without strain, a memory that forgot almost nothing, a flood of illustration, humour and pathos, and a command of plain English that few writers have matched. It is all the more striking, then, that he insisted so relentlessly that none of it could save a single soul. The Word of God was the instrument, and the Spirit of God was the power. Without both, he believed, the finest preaching in London was noise.

A Book to be believed

Spurgeon held the Bible to be the inspired Word of God, true in all it affirms and the final authority for faith and life. He did not argue the point at great length in most of his sermons; he assumed it and preached from it. His method was nearly always to take a text, often a single verse, open it phrase by phrase, and press it on the hearer. The authority of what he said rested, in his own mind, entirely on its being what God had said.

All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness. 2 TIMOTHY 3:16

In a passage gathered in Gleanings Among the Sheaves he notes how the apostles loved to quote the old Scriptures, even though as inspired men they might have used fresh words. They preferred the old words on which the seal of God had already been set. He urges believers to do the same. The words of ministers may be sweet, he says, but the words of God are sweeter, and they will not be found wanting on the day they are needed.

This conviction lay at the root of the Down-Grade controversy, which chapter twenty-two describes. When Spurgeon saw ministers treating Scripture as a merely human book to be corrected by modern thought, he believed the foundation of everything was being removed.

A Book that must be lit

Yet he was equally clear that the Bible could be read, studied and even memorised without profit. In the same collection he writes that you may read the Bible continuously and never learn anything by it unless it is lit up by the Spirit. Then the words shine like stars. “Blind men may read the Bible with their fingers,” he says, “but blind souls cannot.” We need a light to read by, and there is no reading it in the dark.

Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law. PSALM 119:18

He adds a principle that has guided sound interpretation for centuries: “Those who would best know God’s Word, must study it in its own light.” Scripture interprets Scripture. The Spirit who inspired the Book is the Spirit who explains it, and He does so chiefly by leading the reader from one part of it to another.

Christ applied by the Spirit

The same balance governs his teaching on salvation. Spurgeon preached the cross with all his might, but he never imagined that the cross saved anyone automatically. In Gleanings he writes: “Christ on the cross is of no value to us apart from the Holy Spirit in us.” The blood flows in vain, he says, unless the Spirit applies it to the conscience; the robe of righteousness is woven in vain unless the Spirit wraps it round us. We owe as much to the Spirit as to the Son.

Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God. JOHN 3:5

This raised a difficulty for his hearers, and he faced it squarely in All of Grace. If the new birth is the work of God alone, what can a seeker do? Many had despaired at that very point. Spurgeon’s answer is that the same chapter of John which says Ye must be born again also says that whoever believes in the lifted-up Son of Man shall have eternal life. The two must agree. God gives the new birth to all who believe, and their believing is the proof that it has happened. “It is ours to believe,” he writes, “it is the Lord’s to create us anew.” The seeker is not to wait for signs of regeneration before trusting Christ. He is to trust Christ, and find that he has been made new.

The Spirit and the preacher

For Spurgeon this conviction shaped everything about preaching. We have already seen him, at the end of Compel Them to Come In, turning from his hearers to the Spirit: I cannot compel you, but You can. That was not a pious formula. He believed that a sermon was dead until the Spirit gave it life, and that the most eloquent address could leave a congregation untouched while a stammering one, carried by the Spirit, could turn a boy’s life around in a Colchester chapel.

And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:4

In the sermon Christ Crucified he says that nobody truly preaches Christ who leaves out the work of the Holy Spirit. And in his lectures to the students of his college he pressed on them, repeatedly, that their gifts were worthless without the anointing of the Spirit, and that they must seek it in prayer before they sought it anywhere else. It is why the prayer meeting mattered so much to him. The preacher could prepare the fire; only God could send the flame.

Honest questions

Readers today will frame the doctrine of Scripture in different ways, and some will be uneasy with how little patience Spurgeon had for questions of history and criticism. He was a preacher, not a scholar of the text, and he sometimes treated all such questions as unbelief. It is also true, as an earlier chapter noted, that his love of finding Christ everywhere could lead him into readings that the plain sense does not support. But his central convictions stand. Scripture is God’s Word; it must be read in its own light; and it will not open to the proud or the prayerless.

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword. HEBREWS 4:12
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Before you next open your Bible, pray Psalm 119:18 slowly and mean it.

2. Pick a difficult passage you have been puzzling over. Look up the cross-references and let Scripture explain Scripture before you reach for a commentary.

3. Ask whether you have been waiting for some sign of new birth before trusting Christ. Trust Him now, and leave the rest to the Spirit.

4. If you teach or preach, spend as long praying for the Spirit’s help as you spend preparing your material, at least once this month.

5. Memorise one verse this week, and ask the Spirit to use it in your life before the week is out.

A PRAYER
Holy Spirit, without You the Bible is a closed book to me and the cross is a picture on a wall.
Open my eyes to see Christ in Your Word. Apply His blood to my conscience. Clothe me in His righteousness.
Keep me from trusting my own gifts, or the gifts of any preacher. Not by might, nor by power, but by You.
Make the Word I read today live in me, and let it bear fruit to the glory of Jesus. Amen.

fields.title: The Christian Warfare
fields.body_html:
Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ. 2 TIMOTHY 2:3

Spurgeon preached free grace so often and so gladly that some of his critics accused him of making holiness optional. They had not read him carefully. The same man who told the ungodly that God justifies the ungodly told the justified that they were now at war — with the world, with the devil, and above all with the sin that still lived in their own hearts. He saw no tension between the two messages. The grace that forgives is the grace that enlists.

Pardoned and purified

In All of Grace, after several chapters on justification, Spurgeon stops to speak to a particular kind of reader: the person who understands that Christ forgives sin, but whose trouble is that he keeps on sinning. Such a person feels, he says, as if he had a den of wild beasts within him. He has tried to tame them, and they will not be tamed.

Spurgeon’s first word to him is that salvation would be a sadly incomplete affair if it did not deal with this. “Justification without sanctification would not be salvation at all.” It would call the leper clean and leave him to die of his disease. It would pardon the rebel and let him go on as an enemy of the king.

And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins. MATTHEW 1:21

He puts the whole of salvation in one sentence. The Lord Jesus came, he says, “to remove the penalty of sin, the power of sin, and, at last, the presence of sin.” The penalty is removed at once, when we believe. The power of sin may be broken at once too, and its grip begins to loosen from that day. The presence of sin is removed only at the end, when we see Him. The Christian lives between the second and the third, and that is why his life is a war.

A new heart, not a cleaner old one

How is the power of sin broken? Not, Spurgeon says, by resolutions. A man might as well try to hold the north wind in his hand as to tame his fallen nature by his own strength. What is needed is a new nature, and that is what God promises.

A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. EZEKIEL 36:26

He borrows a homely illustration from Rowland Hill. A cat washes itself because it is a cat; a pig wallows because it is a pig. You may scrub a pig, but it will head straight back to the mud. The only way to make a pig wash itself is to turn it into a cat. So it is with the sinner. Reform alone does not last; God must give a new nature, and then what was impossible becomes natural.

This is the great hope of the Christian in his warfare. He does not fight to become a new creature. He fights because he already is one, and the old nature within him no longer rules, though it still rebels.

No kid gloves

When Spurgeon turned to the believer’s war with sin, his language grew fierce. In a passage gathered in Gleanings Among the Sheaves he tells the Christian never to take hold of sin “except with a gauntlet on thy hand; never go to it with the kid-glove of friendship.” Whether sin comes roaring like a lion or creeping like a little fox, whether it is dressed in respectability or applauded by the crowd, it is to be hated everywhere. “Not one sin is to be spared.”

Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth. COLOSSIANS 3:5

He was a realist about what this war would feel like. There is no bed of down for the soldier of Christ, he says, and no riding to heaven in a carriage. Mountains must be climbed and giants fought. And yet the road is pleasant — not because it is easy, but because of the company. The Beloved walks with His soldiers through every thorny place.

Kept in the battle, not out of it

One of his most useful insights concerns how God keeps His people. We tend to imagine that God’s protection means being shielded from temptation. Spurgeon disagreed. “The way that God keeps His people in security,” he writes, “is not by shutting out their enemies from attacking them, but by sustaining them while engaged in the conflict.” God does not grow His plants in a hothouse. He sets them out in the open air, and they are sturdier in summer for the frosts of winter.

There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it. 1 CORINTHIANS 10:13

That is a great comfort to the believer who is ashamed of being tempted at all. Temptation is not proof that God has abandoned you. It is the ground on which He intends to show that He has not.

Honest about the fight

Spurgeon lived in a period when some Christians taught that believers could reach a state of freedom from conscious sin in this life by a single act of consecration. He was wary of such claims, and it shows in his preaching. He knew too well the remaining corruption of his own heart to believe that the war could be ended this side of heaven. He preferred to speak of steady progress, of victories that are real but partial, and of a final triumph that is certain but not yet.

For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other. GALATIANS 5:17

Some readers will find his militant imagery hard to warm to, and it is true that it can be taken in unhealthy directions — towards a grim, suspicious, joyless religion. Spurgeon himself was not joyless. His warfare was fought in the company of a Friend, and he expected the victory. In Gleanings he says that the believer’s battlefield is here, and his triumphal procession above.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Name the sin you have been treating with the kid gloves of friendship. Decide today to take it up only with a gauntlet.

2. Ask whether you have been fighting sin with resolutions alone. Pray Ezekiel 36:26 as a promise, not a wish.

3. When you are tempted this week, remind yourself that temptation is not abandonment. Look for the way of escape God has promised.

4. Distinguish the penalty, the power and the presence of sin. Thank God for the first, ask Him for more victory over the second, and long for the third.

5. Find one fellow believer with whom you can be honest about your battles, and pray for each other.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You came to save me from my sins, not only from their penalty but from their power.
I confess that I have made peace with sins I should be fighting. Put a gauntlet on my hand and a new heart in my breast.
Keep me in the battle, not out of it. When I am tempted, show me the way of escape, and give me the will to take it.
And bring me at last to the day when sin is gone for ever, and I see You as You are. Amen.

fields.title: Why Saints Persevere
fields.body_html:
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. PHILIPPIANS 1:6

There is a fear that keeps many people back from Christ, and Spurgeon met it constantly. It is not the fear that Christ will refuse them. It is the fear that, having come, they will not last. They have made good starts before. They have had seasons of earnestness that faded like morning mist. What if they trust Christ, and then fall away? In the closing chapters of All of Grace Spurgeon turns to this fear, and his answer is one of the most comforting things he ever wrote.

The fear that fulfils itself

He begins with a sharp observation. He believes, he says, that this fear is often the father of the fact. Some who were afraid to trust Christ for all of time did fall away — not because Christ failed them, but because they only half trusted Him. They looked to Him for the beginning and to themselves for the continuing, and so they set out on a faulty foundation. “If we trust to ourselves for our holding on we shall not hold on.”

This is a profound pastoral insight. Many Christians believe that God saved them by grace and now expect to keep themselves saved by effort. They live anxiously, measuring their spiritual temperature, afraid that a bad month might undo everything. Spurgeon says that this is to mix self with the mortar, and it will not hold. “If you look to Christ for your beginnings,” he writes, “beware of looking to yourself for your endings.” He is Alpha; make Him Omega also.

Are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh? GALATIANS 3:3

God is faithful

Where, then, does the believer’s security lie? Spurgeon takes his answer from Paul’s words to the Corinthians: God is faithful, by whom ye were called. Notice, he says, what Paul does not say. He does not say, you are faithful. The faithfulness of man is a very unreliable affair. We are, in Spurgeon’s words, “variable as the wind, frail as a spider’s web, weak as water.” Nor does Paul say that they have faithful ministers to keep them. If we are kept by men, we shall be ill kept.

God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:9

God is faithful to His love, which does not vary. He is faithful to His purpose, and does not begin a work and leave it undone. He is faithful as a Father who will not disown His children, and as a Creator who will not abandon the work of His hands. He is faithful to His covenant, sealed with the blood of His Son, and He will not let that blood be shed in vain. This, Spurgeon says, is the cornerstone of the whole doctrine: “The saints shall persevere in holiness, because God perseveres in grace.”

He adds, with evident pleasure, that this fits the title of his little book. Salvation is all of grace — free favour rings in its dawn, and the same bells sound through the whole of its day.

What God has already done

Spurgeon’s second argument is from what God has already done. He has called His people into the fellowship of His Son, and that call is not reversible. Paul’s chain in Romans 8 has no broken links: those He called, He justified, and those He justified, He glorified.

For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance. ROMANS 11:29

He makes the same point in an earlier chapter about the new heart. When God takes away the heart of stone, the deed is done. Human reformations wear off; the dog returns to its vomit. But when God gives a new heart, it will not harden into stone again. He who made it flesh will keep it so.

And behind the call stands the eternal love that chose, the blood that bought, and the intercession of the living Christ.

Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them. HEBREWS 7:25

Perseverance, not presumption

fields.body_html:
Neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the Lord is your strength. NEHEMIAH 8:10

People who know Spurgeon only from his controversies, or from the darkness described in the next chapter, are sometimes surprised to learn how much he laughed. He was a man of quick wit and hearty humour, and he saw no reason to leave either at the vestry door. In Talks to the Farmer he describes a harvest-home supper at which, when the cheerful meal was ended, he turned one of the tables into a pulpit and preached the gospel in the barn. “My heart was merry in harmony with the occasion,” he says. That merriment was not a lapse from his religion. He believed it was part of it.

A happy Creator, a happy Redeemer

In the passages gathered in Gleanings Among the Sheaves under the heading The Joy of the Christian Life, he states the principle bluntly. “That religion which teaches misery to be a duty is false upon the very face of it.” His argument is from creation. God did not give us only what we need to survive. He gave us flowers in the hedgerow and stars in the sky, beauty that is not strictly useful, because He wished His creatures to be glad.

From this he draws a conclusion that is both simple and profound: “it is not likely that the God who made a happy world would send a miserable salvation.” He who is a happy Creator, he says, will be a happy Redeemer. The gospel is not a grim remedy to be swallowed for the good of our souls. It is good news, and it was meant to make people glad.

Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace. PROVERBS 3:17

It is worth noticing how often Scripture commands joy. Paul does not merely permit the Philippians to rejoice; he tells them to do it, and then tells them again. Spurgeon took such words as seriously as any other command.

Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice. PHILIPPIANS 4:4

Seek Christ first

Yet Spurgeon was no preacher of a cheerful religion for its own sake. He knew that happiness sought directly has a way of slipping through the fingers. His counsel, in the same collection, is precise: “Seek not happiness first; seek Christ first; and happiness shall come after.”

But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you. MATTHEW 6:33

That order matters. A great deal of modern religion promises happiness as its product, and people come to Christ for the sake of the feelings He gives. When the feelings fade, so does their faith. Spurgeon’s joy was of a different kind. It was the by-product of looking at Christ, and so it could survive the loss of almost everything else. In a moving passage he appeals to the poor, the sick, the hard-pressed man of business and the rich, and asks whether their religion had not been a candle in their darkness and a rest in their toil. And he makes a bold claim from long pastoral experience: “Never, never did we know a Christian who repented of his Christianity.” He had seen believers poor, suffering and full of doubts; he had never heard one of them say that he regretted giving himself to Christ.

Where the joy comes from

Spurgeon’s joy was not temperament dressed up as doctrine. He was, as we have seen, a man of deep glooms as well as high spirits. What he rejoiced in were things that did not depend on his mood.

He rejoiced first in pardon. To hear God say, as it were, Son, thy sins are forgiven thee — to wear the best robe and the ring and to hear the music with which the prodigal is welcomed home — was to him a joy that all the pleasures of the world could not match.

Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. PSALM 32:1

He rejoiced next in the settled purposes of God. Commenting on Peter’s words to believers who were in heaviness through manifold temptations, he uses a picture taken from the sea. Mariners, he says, speak of places where a current runs one way on the surface while another runs the opposite way in the depths. “On the surface there is a stream of heaviness rolling in dark waves, but down in the depths there is a strong under-current of great rejoicing.” The Christian can be sad and glad at once, because the deepest things in him — that he is chosen, redeemed and kept for an inheritance that fades not away — are not touched by the weather on the surface.

Wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations. 1 PETER 1:6

And he rejoiced in praise itself. In a passage on the opening of Psalm 103 he calls on his memory, his judgement and his understanding each to find matter for the song, to go back to cradle-mercies and to the hour when he first knew the Lord. All creation praises God, he says. “If I were silent I should be an exception to the universe.”

Bless the Lord, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name. PSALM 103:1

Joy that works

Spurgeon was not interested in a joy that simply sat and enjoyed itself. He noticed that gladness is the best fuel for labour. “It is when the mind is happy that it can be laborious.” A man who serves God grudgingly will soon tire; a man who serves Him gladly will be surprised at how much he can do. The vast web of work that grew around the Tabernacle — the college, the orphanage, the almshouses — was not, in his own understanding, driven by duty alone. It was the overflow of a glad heart.

He had a word, too, for believers who live below their privileges. “Many a believer lives in the cottage of doubt when he might live in the mansion of faith.” The joy is available. It is written in the promises and purchased by the blood. Many Christians simply never move in.

A word of care

There is one sentence in this part of Spurgeon’s teaching that needs handling gently. He writes that a Christian who yields to a mournful, desponding spirit under his trials does dishonour to the noble principles of Christianity. As an encouragement to the fretful, that may be bracing. As a verdict on the clinically depressed, it would be cruel, and Spurgeon, who knew depression from the inside, would not have meant it so. His own life shows that heaviness on the surface is no proof that the undercurrent has stopped. The command to rejoice is not a command to feel cheerful on demand. It is a command to rejoice in the Lord, whose goodness does not rise and fall with our spirits.

Held that way, his teaching is a great gift. The Christian life is not a long face worn for God’s sake. It is the happiest life there is, and the happiness is Christ.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask honestly whether your faith looks, to those who live with you, like good news. What would make it look more so?

2. Take Spurgeon’s counsel literally this week: stop seeking happiness, and seek Christ first in one concrete way each day.

3. Read Psalm 103:1–5 and make your own list of benefits under each heading — forgiveness, healing, redemption, mercy, provision.

4. If you are in heaviness now, name one thing beneath the surface that has not changed: that you are pardoned, chosen, kept. Rejoice in that.

5. Notice where you serve God grudgingly. Ask Him for gladness in that work rather than simply more effort.

A PRAYER
Happy Creator and happy Redeemer, You made a world full of gladness and sent a Saviour to make me glad.
Forgive me for wearing a long face and calling it godliness, and for seeking happiness instead of seeking You.
When the surface of my life is heavy, let the deep current of Your love run on beneath it, strong and unbroken.
Make me glad in Your pardon, glad in Your purposes, glad in Your praise, and let the joy of the Lord be my strength. Amen.

fields.title: Songs in the Night
fields.body_html:
But none saith, Where is God my maker, who giveth songs in the night. JOB 35:10

The Prince of Preachers was often a man in the dark. It surprises people who know only the famous name and the vast congregations, but it is one of the most important things about him. From the night of the Surrey Gardens disaster, when he was twenty-two, to the end of his life, Spurgeon suffered recurring bouts of depression, sometimes with an obvious cause and sometimes with none. He also suffered years of severe physical pain from gout and kidney disease. He did not hide any of this. He preached out of it, and it made him one of the tenderest pastors of the afflicted the church has known.

Any man can sing in the day

His sermon Songs in the Night takes its text from a speech of Elihu in the book of Job. Elihu complains that people in trouble look everywhere for help except to the God who gives songs in the night. Spurgeon thought that true of most Christian distress.

But what he chiefly draws from the text is who the author of such songs must be. “Any man can sing in the day,” he says. When the cup is full and the harvest is in, anybody can praise God. It is easy for a wind harp to make music when the wind is blowing. “It is easy to sing when we can read the notes by daylight, but he is the skillful singer who can sing when there is not a ray of light by which to read.” Such a singer, he says, sings from his heart and not from a book. And only God can put that song there.

Yet the Lord will command his lovingkindness in the daytime, and in the night his song shall be with me, and my prayer unto the God of my life. PSALM 42:8

He also offers a word to those who cannot sing even that. When the present is dark, he says, you may still sing of the past. It is night now, but you can remember when you saw the sun. That is not a small thing. Memory of former mercies is one of the songs God gives in the dark.

A minister who fainted

Spurgeon was most personal about his depression when speaking to the students of his Pastors’ College. In one of the addresses later published in Lectures to My Students, under the title The Minister’s Fainting Fits, he told them plainly that fits of depression come upon most ministers, himself among them, and that they should not be surprised or ashamed. He described how such darkness had fallen on him sometimes before a great work and sometimes after it, sometimes through overwork and sometimes for no reason he could find. He did not treat it as a sin or as evidence of weak faith. He treated it as part of the lot of earthen vessels, which God uses precisely because they are weak.

But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:7

That was a remarkable thing for a famous preacher to say to young men who idolised him, and it has been a lifeline to many sufferers since. Depression was not, for Spurgeon, a failure of doctrine. He knew the doctrines of grace as well as any man alive, and they did not prevent the darkness. What they did was give him somewhere to stand while it lasted.

God in the furnace

In the passages gathered in Gleanings Among the Sheaves under the heading In Sorrow and Affliction, Spurgeon gathers his settled convictions about suffering. The first is that God is present in it. “As sure as ever God puts His children in the furnace,” he writes, “He will be in the furnace with them.” He points to Jacob, who met the angel only when he had to wrestle, and to John, who saw the Revelation on the barren rock of Patmos.

When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned. ISAIAH 43:2

The second conviction is that affliction has a purpose and a limit. God does not afflict willingly. He never keeps His people in the furnace longer than His wise and loving purpose requires, and when that purpose is served He removes the rod. Spurgeon draws this from the end of Job’s story: The Lord turned the captivity of Job. “Our longest sorrows have a close,” he says, “and there is a bottom to the profoundest depths of our misery.”

For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:17

And the third conviction is that God does His best work in His people through suffering. “The Lord gets his best soldiers out of the highlands of affliction.” That sentence is easy to say and very hard to live. Spurgeon lived it.

Deep waters

The preface to the Cheque Book, written in the last years of his life, is one of his most moving pieces of writing, precisely because it is so restrained. He says that since beginning the book he had been cast into waters to swim in which, but for God’s upholding hand, would have been waters to drown in. Sharp bodily pain followed mental depression, and both were accompanied by bereavement and by the illness of one dear to him as life. He mentions it, he says, only so that readers will know that the comfort he offers is not theoretical.

Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him. JOB 13:15

A caution, and a comfort

Spurgeon lived before depression was understood as it is now, and he sometimes spoke of it in wholly spiritual terms. Readers who suffer should not take him to mean that prayer and promises are the only help they may seek. He himself rested when he could, sought the sun of the south of France, and relied on the care of others. Using the means God provides — medical, practical and relational — is not a lack of faith. But his central comfort holds. Darkness is not proof that God has gone. It may be the very place where He intends to give a song.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. If you are in a season of darkness, tell God honestly how it feels. Spurgeon never pretended; you need not either.

2. Write down three mercies from a brighter season of your life. When you cannot sing of the present, sing of those.

3. If your low spirits have lasted a long time, speak to someone you trust, and consider seeing a doctor. Doing so is not a failure of faith.

4. Think of someone you know who is suffering. Visit, write or call them this week, without trying to explain their trouble.

5. Read Psalm 42 slowly, and notice how the psalmist speaks both to God and to his own soul.

A PRAYER
God my Maker, who giveth songs in the night, the night has come and I cannot find the tune.
I remember when I saw the sun. Help me to hold on to that memory until the morning comes.
You are with me in the furnace. You will not keep me there one moment longer than Your love requires.
Give me a song I could never have written myself, and let it comfort others who walk in the dark. Amen.

He described how such darkness had fallen on him sometimes before a great work and sometimes after it, sometimes through overwork and sometimes for no reason he could find. He did not treat it as a sin or as evidence of weak faith. He treated it as part of the lot of earthen vessels, which God uses precisely because they are weak. What they did was give him somewhere to stand while it lasted. He never keeps His people in the furnace longer than His wise and loving purpose requires, and when that purpose is served He removes the rod. Spurgeon draws this from the end of Job’s story: The Lord turned the captivity of Job. “Our longest sorrows have a close,” he says, “and there is a bottom to the profoundest depths of our misery.” For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:17 And the third conviction is that God does His best work in His people through suffering. “The Lord gets his best soldiers out of the highlands of affliction.” That sentence is easy to say and very hard to live. Spurgeon lived it. Deep waters The preface to the Cheque Book, written in the last years of his life, is one of his most moving pieces of writing, precisely because it is so restrained. He says that since beginning the book he had been cast into waters to swim in which, but for God’s upholding hand, would have been waters to drown in. Sharp bodily pain followed mental depression, and both were accompanied by bereavement and by the illness of one dear to him as life. He mentions it, he says, only so that readers will know that the comfort he offers is not theoretical. Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him. JOB 13:15 A caution, and a comfort Spurgeon lived before depression was understood as it is now, and he sometimes spoke of it in wholly spiritual terms. Readers who suffer should not take him to mean that prayer and promises are the only help they may seek. He himself rested when he could, sought the sun of the south of France, and relied on the care of others. Using the means God provides — medical, practical and relational — is not a lack of faith. But his central comfort holds. Darkness is not proof that God has gone. It may be the very place where He intends to give a song. FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. If you are in a season of darkness, tell God honestly how it feels. Spurgeon never pretended; you need not either. 2. Write down three mercies from a brighter season of your life. When you cannot sing of the present, sing of those. 3. If your low spirits have lasted a long time, speak to someone you trust, and consider seeing a doctor. Doing so is not a failure of faith. 4. Think of someone you know who is suffering. Visit, write or call them this week, without trying to explain their trouble. 5. Read Psalm 42 slowly, and notice how the psalmist speaks both to God and to his own soul. A PRAYER God my Maker, who giveth songs in the night, the night has come and I cannot find the tune. I remember when I saw the sun. Help me to hold on to that memory until the morning comes. You are with me in the furnace. You will not keep me there one moment longer than Your love requires. Give me a song I could never have written myself, and let it comfort others who walk in the dark. Amen.

fields.body_html:
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord’s death till he come. 1 CORINTHIANS 11:26

Some of Spurgeon’s warmest words were not spoken to the thousands who filled the Tabernacle on Sunday mornings but to small groups of believers gathered round the Lord’s Table — at the Tabernacle, and in the last winters of his life in his sitting-room at Menton, among Christians of several denominations and nationalities. A selection of these communion addresses was published after his death under the title Till He Come. It is the tenderest of his books, and it shows the centre of his devotional life.

Every Lord’s Day

The editors of Till He Come record that it was Spurgeon’s constant custom, at home or abroad, to break bread every Sunday unless illness prevented, and that he believed this to be the practice of the apostles. They add that his repeated testimony was that the more often he obeyed the command, This do in remembrance of Me, the more precious his Saviour became.

And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me. LUKE 22:19

Many Christians today take communion rarely, and some almost as an afterthought at the end of a long service. Spurgeon regarded the Supper as one of the chief means by which Christ keeps His people near Him. He did not think it worked by magic. He thought it worked by setting Christ crucified before the eyes of faith, week by week, in bread and wine, until the heart was warmed.

A fellowship, not a spectacle

Spurgeon’s view of the Supper was simple, and he defended its simplicity with some heat. In an address at Menton on 1 Corinthians 10:16–17, Communion with Christ and His People, he laments that so plain an ordinance has been overgrown with ceremony, and that some speak of it as if the eating and drinking had a physical or almost magical power in themselves. “Superstition has produced a sacrament where Jesus intended a fellowship.”

What, then, does the Supper mean? It means communion — with Christ, and with one another. And communion, he says, rests on union. We cannot share life with Christ until we are joined to Him. “Union lies at the basis of communion.”

The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? 1 CORINTHIANS 10:16

Readers from traditions with a higher view of the sacrament will find him polemical here, and at times unfair; he could lump together very different Christian understandings under the heading of superstition. Readers of every tradition, however, can share his main concern: that the Supper should lead us to Christ Himself, not stop at the rite.

Many ways of communion

The same address has a passage that deserves to be better known. Spurgeon says that believers have many ways of communion with Christ besides the Table. They speak with Him in prayer, and He speaks with them through His Word. They share His thoughts, delighting in the Father as He does. They share His feelings, grieving over sin and weeping over sinners as He wept over Jerusalem. They share His work, whenever they teach the ignorant or seek the wandering sheep.

He then adds a personal confession. Sometimes in prayer, he says, when he feels unable to say anything, he likes simply to sit still and look up, and faith sees the Well-beloved and hears His voice in the silence. He insists that this is not a dream or a rare rapture. The devout soul, he says, “can converse with the Lord Jesus all the day.”

Truly our fellowship is with the Father, and with his Son Jesus Christ. 1 JOHN 1:3

That is the heart of Till He Come. Spurgeon was a man of immense activity — college, orphanage, magazine, correspondence, sermons weekly in print. Beneath it all was a private life of quiet, affectionate communion with Christ. The Table was the place where that life was renewed.

Christ known should be Christ used

Several of the addresses take their texts from the Song of Solomon, which Spurgeon read, with a long line of Puritans before him, as a picture of the love between Christ and His people. In Under the Apple Tree, on the words I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste, he opens with a sentence that could summarise his whole devotional teaching: “Christ known should be Christ used.”

I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste. SONG OF SOLOMON 2:3

It is a pity, he goes on, that we know so much about Christ and enjoy Him so little. The bride in the Song does not merely know that her Beloved gives shade; she sits in it. She does not merely believe He bears fruit; she tastes it. The best evidence of Christ’s power, Spurgeon says, is to trust Him and be saved oneself.

Not every reader will follow his interpretation of the Song, and it is fair to say that he sometimes pressed its details further than the text will bear. But the application does not depend on the method. The rebuke stands: many Christians are well informed about Christ and scarcely acquainted with Him.

Looking forward

The title of the book comes from Paul: ye do shew the Lord’s death till he come. The Supper looks backward to the cross and forward to the return of Christ. It is a meal for travellers, eaten between two comings. Spurgeon loved that double horizon. The same table that reminds us of the Sin-Bearer promises the marriage supper of the Lamb.

But I say unto you, I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom. MATTHEW 26:29

Many of the Menton addresses were given by a man in failing health, far from his own congregation. They have the quiet glow of someone already looking across the river.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Before you next take communion, spend time the evening before reading one of the Gospel accounts of the Last Supper.

2. At the Table, deliberately look past the bread and cup to Christ Himself. Speak to Him, silently, as to a friend present.

3. Try Spurgeon’s practice this week: in prayer, when words run out, sit still and look up.

4. Ask where you know Christ without using Him. Choose one truth about Him and act on it today.

5. Remember at the Table that it points forward. Thank God that the One who died is coming again.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You said, This do in remembrance of Me, and I have too often done it without remembering You.
Meet me at Your Table. Let the bread and the cup lead me past themselves to You, crucified for me and risen.
I know so much about You and enjoy You so little. Let me sit under Your shadow with great delight, and taste that Your fruit is sweet.
Keep me in communion with You all the day, and keep me looking for the day when I shall drink it new with You in Your Father’s kingdom. Amen.

fields.title: He That Winneth Souls
fields.body_html:
The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise. PROVERBS 11:30

Spurgeon measured his ministry by one standard, and it was not the size of his congregation or the sales of his sermons. It was the number of people brought to Christ. He wanted the same standard applied to every Christian. Winning souls was not, in his view, the specialist task of preachers and missionaries. It was the business of the whole church, and of every believer in it.

The one great aim

In a reading for an evening in December, in the collection now published as Evening by Evening, Spurgeon reflects on Paul’s words, that I might by all means save some. He notes that Paul did not set out to educate the lost or to refine them, but to save them. He saw men sinking and did not talk of improving their manners. Saving souls was his consuming passion, his ambition and his calling. Then Spurgeon turns to the reader. Have we lived to win souls at that rate? If not, why not? “Jesus died for sinners, cannot we live for them?”

I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some. 1 CORINTHIANS 9:22

He warns in the same passage that Christian work can drift towards lesser aims. A church can teach people, entertain them, reform their habits and improve their circumstances, and never bring one of them to Christ. All of that has value; much of it Spurgeon himself did. But of what use will it be at the last day, he asks, to have taught and moralised people if they stand before God unsaved?

Heaven and hell are in earnest

His motives were not complicated. He believed that people without Christ were lost, that judgement was real, and that the gospel was their only hope. In another evening reading, on the words In the evening withhold not thy hand, he urges himself and his readers to spend the spare hours of the day telling others about Jesus. Jesus gave both His hands to the nails; how can I keep back one of mine from His work? And then a line that sums up his urgency: “heaven and hell are in earnest, let me be so.”

Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:11

This is uncomfortable for modern readers, and it should be. Many Christians say they believe in eternal judgement but live as if nobody they know is in any danger. Spurgeon thought that inconsistency was one of the great scandals of the church. He did not mean that we should frighten people into the kingdom. His own preaching was full of tenderness. But he believed that love tells the truth about danger.

And others save with fear, pulling them out of the fire. JUDE 1:23

Motive and manner

Spurgeon’s soul-winning was never mechanical. He had no single method, and he distrusted anything that looked like a technique for producing conversions. He believed that only the Spirit could give life, as chapter fourteen has shown, and that the soul-winner’s part was to be faithful, loving and persistent, and to leave the results with God. He was glad to see others winning souls by methods different from his own, and in Talks to the Farmer he warns against the spirit of the disciples who forbade a man casting out demons because he did not follow with them.

He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him. PSALM 126:6

What he did insist on was earnestness. We have already seen him in Compel Them to Come In pleading with many tears. He could not understand a Christian who believed the gospel and felt no burden for the lost. And he expected that burden to find practical expression: in prayer, in personal conversation, in Sunday-school teaching, in giving away good books, in visiting the sick and the poor.

Every member a worker

The Tabernacle under Spurgeon was an extraordinary hive of activity, and much of it was evangelistic. Members ran Sunday schools and ragged schools, mission halls in poor districts, and meetings for working men and for the poor. Many of the men trained in his Pastors’ College went out to plant new congregations in London and far beyond it. The Colportage Association sent men into villages with Bibles and Christian books to sell and to talk about Christ. Spurgeon did not think of these as the church’s optional extras. He thought of them as the church being the church.

Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature. MARK 16:15

He applied the same standard to his own writing. In the opening pages of All of Grace he says that he will be greatly disappointed if the book does not lead many to the Lord Jesus, and he adds a prayer that some of its readers might themselves become great winners of souls. Every book, every sermon, every institution was meant to multiply the work.

To the last hour

In the evening reading on Ecclesiastes 11:6, Spurgeon speaks of the evening of life as well as the evening of the day. Some are spared to a long old age, he says; if that is his lot, he wants to use whatever gifts remain to serve his Lord to the last. “By his grace I will die in harness, and lay down my charge only when I lay down my body.” He was granted no long old age. He died at fifty-seven. But he died in harness.

And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever. DANIEL 12:3

A word of balance

It is fair to say that Spurgeon’s urgency, taken without his tenderness, can become harsh, and that some who have imitated his language of hell and judgement have not imitated his tears. It is also fair to say that the church has sometimes set evangelism against care for the poor, as if one must choose. Spurgeon did not. The next chapter shows how the same Tabernacle that preached for souls built an orphanage and almshouses. But he never let works of mercy replace the gospel, and he never let doctrine excuse silence.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask honestly whether your Christian activity is aimed at people being saved, or at something lesser. What would change if it were aimed at the highest thing?

2. Write down the names of three people you know who do not know Christ. Pray for each by name every day this month.

3. Look for one opportunity this week to speak naturally about what Christ means to you.

4. Consider giving away a good Christian book — All of Grace was written for exactly this purpose — to someone who might read it.

5. If you have grown older, ask Spurgeon’s question of yourself: what gifts remain that could still be used in harness?

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You died for sinners, and I have hardly lived for them.
Forgive me for believing in heaven and hell and yet behaving as if nobody I know were in danger. Give me earnestness, and give me tenderness.
Use my words, my prayers, my home and my hands to bring others to You. Keep me from mistaking busyness for fruitfulness.
And let me serve You to the last hour, and lay down my work only when I lay down my body. Amen.

fields.body_html:

Around the pulpit of the Metropolitan Tabernacle grew a remarkable cluster of institutions: a college for training preachers, an orphanage, almshouses for poor widows, a society for carrying Christian books into the villages, a fund for supplying poor ministers with books, Sunday schools, mission halls and a monthly magazine. He did not regard any of this as a distraction from preaching the gospel. He regarded it as the gospel at work.

The best-known of these works began with a gift. In 1866 a widow named Anne Hillyard wrote to Spurgeon offering a large sum to found an orphanage for fatherless boys. Spurgeon had been praying about such a work. The Stockwell Orphanage was founded the following year in south London, and in time received girls as well as boys. It was arranged not as a great barracks but as a group of houses, each a kind of family home. Later in life Spurgeon could use it quite naturally as a sermon illustration. The poor at the door

The orphanage was only one work among many. The Tabernacle maintained almshouses for elderly women of the congregation who had no other support. Its members ran ragged schools, Sunday schools and mission stations in some of the poorest parts of London. The Colportage Association employed men to go into country districts with Bibles and good books, selling them cheaply and speaking about Christ as they went. He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord; and that which he hath given will he pay him again. PROVERBS 19:17

None of this was new in principle. The church has cared for widows and orphans since the days of the apostles. What is striking is that Spurgeon, whose whole theology insisted that works cannot save, was so tireless in good works. He saw no contradiction. In a passage gathered in Gleanings Among the Sheaves he writes that “our good works spring from union with Christ.” The branch bears fruit not in order to become a branch, but because it is one.

For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them. EPHESIANS 2:10

Men for the ministry

The work closest to his heart was the Pastors’ College. It began in 1856 with a single student, a young man whom Spurgeon undertook to teach and support himself, and grew until it had trained hundreds of ministers. Spurgeon deliberately took men that other colleges would not: those without money or social standing or a good education, but with evident gifts and zeal for the gospel. He had been such a man himself. Students paid nothing; for years much of the cost came from his own income. And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also. 2 TIMOTHY 2:2

Many of these men went out to plant churches in London, where new congregations sprang up across the city, and others went to the countries of the empire and beyond. Spurgeon considered the college his greatest work, because it multiplied the preaching of the gospel far beyond anything one voice could do.

What this asks of a church

Spurgeon’s example presses a question on every congregation. What does our faith build? A church can be orthodox in its preaching and do nothing for the fatherless or the poor on its own doorstep. Spurgeon would have regarded that as a contradiction of the gospel it preached. He also presses the opposite question. A church can be busy in good works and forget to preach Christ. He would have regarded that as a building without a foundation.

Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven. MATTHEW 5:16

Honest limits

It is only fair to say that Spurgeon worked within the assumptions of his age. His charity was generous and personal, but it rarely questioned the conditions that made so many people poor, and some modern readers will find its tone paternal. It is also true that the load he carried — preaching, writing, editing, fund-raising and overseeing a dozen institutions — contributed to the breakdowns in health that shortened his life. He is not a model of how to rest. But he is a model of how grace, truly received, spills over into the lives of the needy, and of a man who would not preach a mercy he was unwilling to practise.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask what your faith has built, or helped to build, for someone who could never repay you.

2. Find out who the fatherless, the widowed or the poor are in your own congregation or neighbourhood. Take one practical step to help one of them this month.

3. Give something this week that requires you to trust God, as Spurgeon did when the orphanage funds were low.

4. If you are in a position to teach or train others, ask whom you should be investing in, as Spurgeon invested in his students.

5. Examine whether your church leans towards words without works, or works without the Word. Pray for both to be held together.

A PRAYER
Father of the fatherless and judge of the widows, You have shown mercy to me who had nothing, and I have been slow to show it to others.
Let my faith not be words only. Let it build something for those who cannot repay.
Give me the courage to hang on Your bare arm, and to give when I cannot see how the need will be met.
Keep Your church preaching Christ and practising His mercy, until He comes. Amen.

fields.title: The Down Grade
fields.body_html:
Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints. JUDE 1:3

The last great public struggle of Spurgeon’s life began in 1887 and was not over when he died. It divided him from the denomination in which he had served for more than thirty years, cost him many friendships, including some with men he had trained, and almost certainly hastened the decline of his health. It is known as the Down-Grade controversy, after the title of a series of articles in his magazine. No chapter in this book calls for more care, because it shows Spurgeon at his most courageous and at his most combative, and the two are not easily separated.

What alarmed him

In the 1880s a number of Nonconformist ministers in England, influenced by new ways of reading the Bible and by the general optimism of the age, were quietly setting aside doctrines that earlier generations had taken for granted. Some questioned the full inspiration of Scripture. Some spoke of the atonement as an example of love rather than a substitution for sinners. Some doubted that anyone would finally be lost. The phrase used for this movement was modern thought, and Spurgeon had been warning against it for years. In the communion address The Sin-Bearer he speaks of a teaching of modern thought that explains away the doctrine of substitution, and he answers it sharply: if we lose the cross, we have lost all.

For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears. 2 TIMOTHY 4:3

In 1887 The Sword and the Trowel published articles, some by a friend and some by Spurgeon himself, arguing that the churches were on a down grade: that the slide from evangelical truth was accelerating, and that ministers who had abandoned the gospel were being tolerated, even honoured, within the Baptist Union. Spurgeon pressed the Union to adopt a clear evangelical statement of faith. When it would not do so on his terms, he withdrew from it, in October 1887.

The cost

The response was bitter. In January 1888 the Council of the Baptist Union passed a vote of censure on him, on the ground that he had made charges without naming the men he accused. He had declined to name individuals publicly, which his friends thought honourable and his opponents thought unfair. The Union later adopted a doctrinal statement, but one loose enough to satisfy both sides of the dispute, and Spurgeon regarded it as worthless. Old friends parted from him. A good number of former students of his own college remained in the Union. He reconstituted the conference of his college’s former students on a clear doctrinal basis, and some would not join it.

At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me: I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge. 2 TIMOTHY 4:16

What it cost him inwardly can be glimpsed in the preface to the Cheque Book. He began those daily readings, he says, “when I was wading in the surf of controversy.” He speaks of bearing the Lord’s reproach outside the camp. And he says that the words of God to Jeremiah had become exceedingly sweet to him, because the prophet had to speak to those who would not hear. Jeremiah’s, he writes, “was the sorrow which comes of disappointed love, and resolute loyalty.” It is hard to read that sentence without hearing Spurgeon describing himself.

Why he fought

It would be easy to dismiss the Down Grade as an older man’s rearguard action against a changing world. That would be a mistake. Spurgeon was not defending a set of opinions for their own sake. He was defending the gospel he had preached for forty years — the inspiration of Scripture, the substitution of Christ, the need for new birth, the reality of judgement. If those went, he believed, there would be nothing left to offer the miserable boy under the gallery. In a reading in Morning by Morning he speaks of Christians standing outside the camp as witnesses for the truth, “loving Christ first, and his truth next, and Christ and his truth beyond all the world.” That order matters. Truth mattered to him because Christ mattered to him.

Buy the truth, and sell it not. PROVERBS 23:23

Many later observers have concluded that he read the direction of travel accurately. Much of English Nonconformity did move a long way from the gospel he preached in the generations after his death.

Where he may be questioned

And yet honesty requires more than that. Spurgeon was a fighter by temperament, and he had been one long before 1887. His sermon on baptismal regeneration in 1864 had set off a storm with evangelical clergy in the Church of England, many of whom were his allies in the gospel. In the Down-Grade controversy his language was often sweeping. He could give the impression that all who stayed in the Union were compromised, when many of them held exactly his beliefs and simply judged that the fight was best fought from within. His refusal to name the men he accused, whatever its motives, left his charges hard to answer and easy to resent. And the withdrawal, however principled, removed the strongest evangelical voice from the counsels of his denomination at the moment it was most needed.

But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ. EPHESIANS 4:15

The lesson for readers is not that Spurgeon was wrong to contend. Jude tells us to contend earnestly. It is that contending well is very hard, and that even a godly man with a just cause can wound brethren who deserved better. Truth and love are not rivals. But in the heat of controversy one is always tempted to let the first excuse the absence of the second.

His last word

His last address to the conference of his college, in 1891, later printed as The Greatest Fight in the World, did not rehearse the controversy. It spoke of the Word as the preacher’s armoury, the church as his army, and the Holy Spirit as his strength. He did not recant, and he did not gloat. He urged them to preach the old gospel and to rely on the old power. He had lost a great deal. He had not lost the thing he fought for.

I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith. 2 TIMOTHY 4:7
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask which truths you would be willing to lose friendships over. Ask also which lesser things you have treated as if they were such truths.

2. If you are in a disagreement with other Christians, examine your words. Could the people you are opposing recognise themselves fairly in what you say about them?

3. Read Jude slowly. Notice that it both commands contending and ends in mercy, building up and praying for others.

4. Pray for your own church and denomination, that it would hold fast to the gospel without becoming harsh.

5. If you have been wounded in a church conflict, bring it to Christ, who bore reproach outside the camp, and ask for grace not to become bitter.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You are the truth, and You call me to contend for the faith once delivered to the saints.
Give me courage to stand when the gospel is at stake, and humility to know when it is not.
Keep me from harshness in the name of faithfulness, and from cowardice in the name of peace.
When I must go outside the camp, let it be for Your sake and bearing Your reproach, and let me go in love. Amen.
