fields.title: For Ever with the Lord
fields.body_html:
For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first … and so shall we ever be with the Lord. 1 THESSALONIANS 4:16–17

Spurgeon lived much of his life in pain, and it shows in how he wrote about heaven. He did not think of it as a vague reward or a pleasant idea at the end of a sermon. He thought of it as home, and he longed for it the way a traveller on a long, hard road longs for his own front door. The longing grew stronger as the years went on, the gout grew worse and the controversy grew more bitter. Yet it never made him idle or gloomy. His hope of heaven was one of the springs of his energy on earth.

Bread of grace, wine of glory

In the Cheque Book he comments on a verse from the Psalms: The Lord will give grace and glory. Grace is what we need now, he says, and it is freely given day by day. And then he stops on the little word between them. What an and is that! We do not need glory yet, and we are not yet fit for it, but it will come in its due order. “After we have eaten the bread of grace, we shall drink the wine of glory.”

For the Lord God is a sun and shield: the Lord will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly. PSALM 84:11

That sentence holds his whole view of the Christian life. The present is a meal of grace, sufficient for each day. The future is a feast. The one leads to the other as surely as the first course leads to the second. The believer does not have to choose between enjoying God now and hoping in Him later. He enjoys Him now, and the enjoyment is itself a foretaste.

An inheritance, not a wage

Spurgeon was careful to say that heaven, like everything else in salvation, is all of grace. In a passage gathered in Gleanings Among the Sheaves he reflects on the phrase the inheritance of the saints. An inheritance, he points out, “is not a thing which is bought with money, earned by labor, or won by conquest.” It comes by birth. So it is with heaven. It belongs to those who have been born again into God’s family, not as servants who have earned wages but as sons and daughters who are heirs.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you. 1 PETER 1:3–4

This guards heaven from becoming another source of anxiety. The believer does not wonder whether he has done enough to deserve it. Nobody deserves it. It is given, and because it is given, it is sure.

Like unto His glorious body

The passages in which Spurgeon writes about the resurrection of the body are among the most personal he wrote, because he wrote them from a body that often failed him. In the Cheque Book, on the promise that Christ will change our vile body to be fashioned like His glorious body, he speaks of being so racked with pain that he could neither think nor worship. And then he looks forward: in a little while we shall be as Jesus now is. “No more aching brows, no more swollen limbs, no more dim eyes, no more fainting hearts.”

Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body. PHILIPPIANS 3:21

Anyone who has suffered long illness will feel the weight of that. It is not escapism. Spurgeon worked through his pain for decades. It is the hope that makes the pain bearable, because it is not the last word.

He could also speak gently of death itself. In Gleanings he describes it, for the believer, as a sleep: the tired body resting at last, the worker laying down his tools, the hand still, the feet no longer sore — until the Lord wakes His people to give them their full reward.

He is coming

Spurgeon believed that Christ would return in person, visibly and gloriously, to raise the dead, judge the world and make all things new. The title of his communion addresses, Till He Come, expresses the hope that framed every Lord’s Supper he shared. He held views about the order of the last things that not every Christian shares, and readers need not follow him in the details. What is worth noticing is that, unlike many in his day, he was not given to prophetic speculation or date-setting. The fact of the return mattered more to him than the timetable.

Behold, he cometh with clouds; and every eye shall see him. REVELATION 1:7

The practical effect of this hope, for him, was twofold. It made him watchful: a servant who expects his master does not sleep on the job. And it made him glad: the Bridegroom is coming for His bride.

Christ is the heaven of heaven

In a reading in Morning by Morning Spurgeon borrows a saying of the Scottish Puritan Samuel Rutherford: that heaven and Christ are the same thing. That is the key to all he believed about the life to come. Heaven was not chiefly golden streets or reunions with loved ones, though he spoke of both. It was being with Christ, without the veil of sin or the weight of the body. The One he had looked to as a boy in Colchester he would at last see face to face.

Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory. JOHN 17:24

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. HEBREWS 12:2

Twenty-one chapters can make it seem that Charles Spurgeon taught a great many things. He taught one thing, and everything else is that one thing applied. Salvation is all of grace, and grace is received by looking to Jesus Christ crucified. Follow it through and the whole structure appears. God justifies the ungodly, because Christ bore their sins in His own body. That is why every sermon must end at the cross. Grace is sovereign, so nobody can boast; grace is free, so anybody may come. Faith is simply the hand that takes it, and repentance is its companion, given by the same exalted Christ. The God who gives it does not change, so the promises are cheques drawn on grace; prayer presents them. The Word reveals Christ and the Spirit applies Him. The war with sin is fought by those whom grace has made new, and they persevere because God perseveres. Grace makes them glad, and in the night, grace gives a song. At the Table, grace sets Christ before the eye again. And grace sends the church out to the lost and the poor, makes it contend for the gospel that saved it, and brings it home at last to see the One it has been looking at all along.

The danger of this book

If you have read this far, you are in some danger, and Spurgeon would have been the first to say so. He was surrounded all his life by admirers — people who could quote his sermons, imitate his style, and defend his doctrines, and who had never themselves looked to Christ. It is entirely possible to become an enthusiast for Spurgeon and remain unconverted. It is possible to enjoy his illustrations, collect his sayings and argue for his Calvinism, and never once take the watch that is held out.

But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. JAMES 1:22

So the plainest counsel this book can give is the same as in its companion volumes. Go back to the chapter that made you least comfortable, not the one you found most interesting. Take its application points and work at them slowly, over weeks. Then take the next.

Two things to carry

First, look. Whatever your condition — anxious or careless, new to faith or long in it, rejoicing or in the dark — the counsel is the same. Stop looking at yourself, and look to Christ. It is the first thing a sinner must do and the last thing a saint will do, and every day between is meant to be lived the same way.

Second, hold together what Spurgeon held together. He believed in the sovereignty of God and pleaded with sinners as if everything depended on it. He preached justification by faith alone and built orphanages. He contended fiercely for truth and wept over the lost. He knew deep depression and wrote about songs in the night. Most of us manage one half of each pair and neglect the other. He was not always balanced, but he refused to let go of either end.

A last word about the man

We have been honest in these pages about his faults. He could be combative to the point of wounding brethren who deserved better, and the Down-Grade controversy was not conducted without harshness on his side. He could speak dismissively of Christians who read Scripture differently on election or the sacraments. His rhetoric belongs to its age and sometimes grates on ours. His readings of the Old Testament could run past the text. And the sheer volume of what he produced means that a good deal of it is repetitive, and some of it is careless.

None of that has been raised to diminish him. It has been raised because his own gospel requires it. A man who taught that he had not a thread of goodness of his own, and who owed everything to grace, cannot be honoured by pretending he was faultless. He would have hated the pretence. He wanted nobody to look at him.

For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus’ sake. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:5

He died at Menton, far from the Tabernacle, at fifty-seven, worn out by work, pain and controversy. On his coffin, as it passed through the streets of London, lay his Bible, open at the text that had saved him: Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth. That was his whole message, and he preached it to the end. It is still being preached, in languages he never heard, to people he never imagined, and it is still enough.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Return to the sentence you wrote at the start of this book about how a person is saved. How would you change it now?

2. Choose the one chapter that searched you most. Reread it, and commit to its application points for the next month.

3. Name the pair of truths you find hardest to hold together — sovereignty and invitation, grace and works, truth and love — and ask God to help you keep both.

4. Put down this book and pick up one of Spurgeon’s own. All of Grace is the best place to begin.

5. Tell someone else where to look.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, I have read about a man who spent his whole life pointing to You. Do not let me stop at admiring the finger.
I look to You now — not to my feelings, my progress, my doctrine or my failures, but to You, lifted up for me.
Hold together in me what I am so quick to separate: truth and love, grace and good works, Your sovereignty and my urgency.
And keep me looking until faith becomes sight, and I see You as You are. Amen.

fields.title: A Reader’s Guide to Charles H. Spurgeon
fields.body_html:
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. 2 TIMOTHY 2:15

Spurgeon is the easiest of the great preachers to read and the hardest to read well. His sentences are vivid, his illustrations homely, and almost everything he wrote is in the public domain and freely available. The difficulty is quantity. Thousands of sermons, dozens of books and a seven-volume commentary make an ocean, and many readers wade in at random and give up. This guide is arranged to save time.

Begin here

All of Grace. Written for seekers late in his life; the best single door into his teaching. In the Ochorus library. Around the Wicket Gate. A companion to All of Grace for those who are anxious and hesitating, full of plain illustrations. In the Ochorus library. The sermons. Rather than attempting the collected volumes, begin with a handful of the best-loved: Compel Them to Come In, Christ Crucified, Free Grace, The Immutability of God, Songs in the Night and The Sinner’s Friend are all in the Ochorus library, among eighteen of his sermons there.

For daily reading

Morning by Morning and Evening by Evening. Two readings for every day of the year, later bound together as Morning and Evening, and never out of print. Rich, occasionally florid, best taken slowly. Both in the Ochorus library. The Cheque Book of the Bank of Faith. A promise and a page of comment for each day, written in the hardest years of his life. More personal than Morning and Evening. In the Ochorus library.

On prayer and communion

Mighty Power in Prayer. A dozen of his sermons on prayer, gathered in the Ochorus library, including The Golden Key of Prayer and Order and Argument in Prayer. Till He Come. His communion addresses, published after his death, many given in his sitting-room at Menton. The tenderest of his books. In the Ochorus library.

Plain talk and gathered wisdom

Talks to the Farmer. Sermons drawn from the fields and the harvest, preached for country people and still fresh; the Ochorus library also holds versions for teens and children. Gleanings Among the Sheaves. Short extracts gathered by theme, useful for dipping into, though the brevity sometimes loses the argument. Both in the Ochorus library. John Ploughman’s Talk. Proverbial wisdom in a rustic voice; very popular in its day, and its humour is of its time.

For preachers and teachers

Lectures to My Students. His Friday afternoon addresses to the men of the Pastors’ College; among the most useful books on preaching ever written, and home to The Minister’s Fainting Fits. The Soul Winner, published after his death, gathers his counsel on evangelism. The Treasury of David, his commentary on the Psalms, is a work of many years and many volumes; it is best consulted alongside one’s own reading of a psalm rather than read through.

Approach with care

The collected sermons. The New Park Street Pulpit and The Metropolitan Tabernacle Pulpit run to more than sixty volumes. Some of the finest preaching in the language, and much repetition. Read by topic or text, not from volume one. The Down-Grade papers. Worth reading to understand chapter twenty-two, but best read alongside a balanced account of the controversy, since they give only his side. The addresses on the Song of Solomon. Rich in devotion, but his interpretation runs further than the text and should be held loosely.

About Spurgeon

His Autobiography, compiled after his death by Susannah Spurgeon and his secretary from his own diaries, letters and records, is the fullest source; the Banner of Truth abridgement in two volumes, The Early Years and The Full Harvest, is more manageable. Arnold Dallimore’s Spurgeon: A New Biography (1985) is short, warm and readable. Lewis Drummond’s Spurgeon: Prince of Preachers (1992) is far fuller. Iain Murray’s The Forgotten Spurgeon (1966) focuses on his theological battles and is openly sympathetic to his side. Zack Eswine’s Spurgeon’s Sorrows (2014) is a gentle book on his depression for those who suffer. Read more than one. Most lives of Spurgeon were written by admirers, and it shows in what they leave out.

Three counsels for reading him

Read him with the Bible open. Spurgeon preached from texts, and his authority rests on them. Check them. Read him for his heart rather than his system. Where he presses a doctrine harder than Scripture does, or speaks more harshly than love requires, take the burden and leave the edge.

And read him to be changed, not merely delighted. He is so enjoyable that it is easy to finish a sermon admiring the preacher. He wanted you to finish it looking at Christ.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21
